Booyzen, Falco, Defranceski and D'Arcy, the difference is not in the data - it
is in what gets checked. Blazevic has 26 tools, Mazza 40-odd; Lerena had 6.
Two siblings carry a check this one did not:
- Blazevic consistency.py - "check the tree against itself, no external source,
  just dates that cannot all be true at once". Its header records the cost:
  Tereza Pecanic published as dying in 1850, marrying in 1858 and bearing
  children until 1884.
- Booyzen drift.py - "catch a narrative page that has fallen behind the data".
BOTH OF THOSE FAILURES HAPPENED HERE TODAY, independently, and both were found
by eye. The sources page had fallen three days behind the work. Three published
dates were wrong - Ema Sixta c.1880 for 1876, Julia c.1844 for 1842, and two
siblings indexed as born in February and July of the same year 1843.
So tools/consistency.py now exists here too. It checks for a parent younger
than their child, full siblings born less than nine months apart, a field that
is both hedged and precise, and a row claiming IMAGE READ while naming no ark.
Contradictions fail the build; softer observations print and do not. Both hard
checks were verified by feeding it synthetic contradictions - two failures,
exit 1 - rather than trusting a clean pass. The deploy now runs it.
IT IMMEDIATELY FOUND FIVE ROWS that say IMAGE READ and carry no ark: Bartolome
Llerena, Julia Juanico, Ema Sixta, Juliana Joaquina Gonzalez and Sancho
Llerena. Those images were genuinely read - but without the ark a reader cannot
check them, and checkability is the entire point of this archive. Logged as an
errand rather than quietly excused.
ITEM 5, the register sweep, found the register structurally clean across all
183 rows - no malformed field counts, no unpaired emphasis markers, no missing
sources, six consistent status values - and one CONTRADICTION WITH A NOTE:
The 1869 census note said Bartolome Llerena was "the only person of this
surname found in Rosario before 1882". SIX LORENAS ARE IN THE SAME CENSUS, and
this archive's own register groups LORENA with LERENA and LLERENA as spellings
of one name, because the clerks disagreed. Two of them - Guillermo b.1853 and
Geronima b.1854 - are flagged in that very register as the right age to be a
parent of a child born in 1882. The note now claims only what was checked, and
the Lorenas stay in view instead of being defined out of the question. Reading
them at their own census pages is now an errand.
ITEM 13: Carolina Lerena married JULIAN MARTINEZ, with children Julian and
Carlos, appearing in Buenos Aires civil registration and Mendoza parish records
- and in Mendoza she is indexed once as Carolina LLERENA, the same alternation
again. Index-level. The 1892 Buenos Aires probate is still not opened.
Register: 179 people -> 183.

commits.subject: Julia's baptism, and Candido Juanico's two wives confirmed
commits.body:
Item 8 of fifteen, closed, plus the inference the archive could not prove.
JULIA JUANICO WAS BORN 23 NOVEMBER 1842 and christened 4 October 1843 at San
Francisco de Asis - the same parish where she married in 1864, where her son
Candido Jaime was baptised in 1886, and where her daughter Maria married that
November. Four generations pass through one church in the Ciudad Vieja. Her
mother is given in full for the first time: JULIANA JOAQUINA GONZALEZ.
Godparents D. Enrique Juanico and Mercedes Gonzalez, both new people.
The 1844 this archive carried came from her stated age at death. She was 67,
not 66. An age at death is an estimate; a baptism is a date.
TWO WIVES, CONFIRMED. The register note on Juliana Gonzalez had read: the
published genealogy gives Candido's wife as SIXTA Lenguas Gonzalez, married
1857 - too late for a daughter marrying in 1864, so Juliana is an earlier wife,
and that is an inference. The inference was right. Searching Candido as a
FATHER returns two clean sets: Julia, born 1842 to Juliana Joaquina Gonzalez;
and Sara, Zara Sista Emirena and Celia JUANICO LENGUAS, born 1866-69 to SIXTA
LENGUAS. A full generation apart. The published genealogy was right about the
marriage and wrong to attach it to Julia.
AND NOTE THE SECOND WIFE'S SURNAME. Candido Juanico's second wife was a
LENGUAS, and his daughter by his first wife married a Lerena LENGUAS. Justiniana
Lenguas and Sixta Lenguas are very likely kin, which would mean these families
were connected before 1864. Recorded as an observation, not a relationship - no
record read here links the two women directly.
One more echo, offered as nothing more: Candido's daughter by Sixta is "Zara
Sista EMIRENA Juanico", and Julia's eldest - the Rosario child of 1866 - is
"Maria Julia Margarita Josefa EMIRENA Justiniana". The half-sisters were given
an uncommon name within a few years of each other.
The roadmap's Montevideo section is rewritten to today: seven children, the
1901 death, the 1843 baptism, and Gilberto in the generation above.
Register: 173 people -> 179.

commits.subject: His death was hiding under an S, and Gilberto is his brother
commits.body:
Items 7 and 14 of fifteen, both closed, and one correction to work published
three hours ago.
THE DEATH IS FOUND: 24 DECEMBER 1901. Luis Eugenio Lerena Lenguas died at
seven in the morning at calle Suarez 25, el Paso del Molino, Montevideo -
certificate 216, image read at DeepZoom level 13. The window had been July 1886
to July 1910.
AND THIS ARCHIVE HAD JUST PUBLISHED THAT HE WAS NOT THERE. Two sweeps were run
this morning and written up as negatives: 1,502 Montevideo Lerena deaths for
1880-1911, and 132 Luis Lerena deaths for 1899-1903. I went further and framed
the FamilySearch Tree's "1840-1901" as a lead the registers appeared to
contradict. The registers did not contradict it. The index did - FamilySearch
files him as "Luis SERENA Lenguas", and every search on the surname missed him.
He was found by searching his MOTHER. For a family the clerks and indexers
between them write as Lerena, Lorena, Serena, Languas, Lenquas, Loupuan and
Guanico, the rarest stable name in the household is the one to search. The
working rule is now written down: when a search fails, suspect the index before
concluding the record does not exist.
WHAT THE ACT GIVES. "De nacionalidad oriental, nacido en Montevideo, de
cincuenta y seis de edad, de estado casado, y de profesion HACENDADO" - a
landowner, the first statement of this family's standing anywhere in the
archive; the Rosario act of 1866 managed only "naturales del E. Oriental".
Pulmonary tuberculosis, certified by Dr Scremini. His father already dead. And
his mother JUSTINIANA LENGUAS ALIVE AT 79, staying in the house where he died -
which puts her birth about 1822 and has her outliving him.
"De estado casado" locks this act to Julia's of 1910, where she is a widow.
GILBERTO LERENA IS HIS BROTHER. The same eight rows returned four siblings -
Justinia (1843), Alberto Otario (1850), Maria Ema (1857) - and two records of
Gilberto's own children, BOTH giving his parents as Luis and Justiniana
Lenguas. So the co-founder of the Argentine Stud Book, owner of Haras El Viejo,
the man the Gran Premio Gilberto Lerena was renamed for in 1914, is of the same
Montevideo household that produced the single Lerena baptised at Rosario before
1879. The horses and the Rosario thread are one family, not two coincidences.
Stated as SECONDARY and as a strong lead, not a proved descent: two parish
index entries agree, and neither image has been opened. It also does not find
Juan Carlos - five siblings named in that generation and none is he - and it
does not yet connect Pablo Armando to any of them.
Register: 170 people -> 173.

commits.subject: Rebuild the changelog, and narrow the emphasis guard to paired markers
commits.body:
A lone *** in prose is not an unconverted field - the TSV convention is always
paired - and flagging it would train me to ignore the check.

commits.subject: A seventh child, four grandparents, and the Trinidad kindred put in the register
commits.body:
Items 4 and 7-9 of fifteen. Item 4 was meant to be a small usability fix to
the register. Testing the page's own search placeholder broke the whole thing
open.
THE PLACEHOLDER WAS LYING TOO. The register's search box invited readers to
try "Trinidad" - and returned nothing, because the entire Trinidad, Flores
kindred was missing from a register that promises "every named individual this
archive has found". This archive has a whole note calling them the founding
kindred of the surname. They are now in it: 29 people. The placeholder is
honest because the data caught up with the promise, not because the promise
was softened.
Re-read from FamilySearch by BIRTHPLACE rather than surname, which produced
what the old findmypast list never gave - the mothers' surnames (Pelaez,
Echeverry, Gazo, Beloqui, Barragan, Recuero) and a seventh father, Florencio.
BELOQUI, ECHEVERRY and PELAEZ ARE BASQUE. That is evidence about the community
these Lerenas married into; it is not evidence about the etymology, and it is
recorded as the former and not the latter.
AND IT CORRECTED US. The note had "Luis x Julia, Emma Liseta 1876" among the
Trinidad families, linking the Montevideo trunk to the Trinidad kindred. She is
Emma Sixta Lerena Juanico, born and baptised at MONTEVIDEO - our own trunk. The
row came off a findmypast list that gives mothers by first name only. The
note's prose had always said eleven Trinidad children while its table showed
twelve; nobody had reconciled the two. Removing her makes the count agree and
severs a link this archive never had.
SEVEN CHILDREN, NOT FIVE. The five were built outward from Julia's 1910 death
certificate - and a death certificate names the children who mattered to
whoever registered the death, not the children a woman bore. Searching both
parents' names in one query found Jose Julio (b. 15 Mar 1879) and Candido Jaime
(b. 13 Sep 1884).
ACT 1720 IS THE BEST DOCUMENT IN THE MONTEVIDEO FILE. San Francisco de Asis,
folio 470, read at DeepZoom level 12. Candido Jaime, baptised 6 July 1886 at
twenty-one months, "hijo legitimo de Don Luis Lerena Lenguas y de Dona Julia
Juanico, ORIENTALES". It names four grandparents, and so:
- It CLOSES an open question. Candido Juanico's wife was JULIANA GONZALEZ, not
  the Sixta Lenguas Gonzalez of the published genealogy. Three acts in one
  parish now say so across twenty-two years.
- The godparents are the baby's own eldest sister Maria - born at Rosario in
  1865 - and Don Jaime Herrera, whom she married in this same parish four
  months later. They stood at the font betrothed.
- He was baptised at 21 months, not as an infant. The whole search for Pablo
  Armando assumes a baptism near the birth.
The FamilySearch index of act 1720 was made by a computer. It filed the act
under LORENA, rendered the father as "Luis Lorena", and marked BOTH parents as
Mother. Searching LERENA and trusting the index would never have found this
child. The image settles it.
Still no Juan Carlos. Seven children and he is not among them - worth more
than it looks, since this was the strongest remaining place to put him.
Register: 139 people -> 170. Site: 198 pages -> 230.

commits.subject: Generate the sources page from data, and stop printing raw markers at readers
commits.body:
1-3 of fifteen. All three are corrections to this archive's own work.
THE SOURCES PAGE WAS LYING. Its "Consulted" table listed 12 sources, newest
10 September, and had not moved for three days - while the Montevideo
household, the Rosario death index, 750 acts of the 1882 register, the
full-text density measurement and Sancho's six spellings all went unrecorded.
The heading above it said "Everything consulted so far". On a page whose whole
purpose is letting a reader check the work, that was a false claim.
It is now generated from data/sources-consulted.tsv - 33 sources, 13 of them
PRIMARY, each carrying its tier - the way people, gaps, errands and changes
already work. The archive's method is that pages are generated from the TSVs
so page and data cannot drift; /sources/ had escaped it.
362 LITERAL ASTERISKS. The TSVs mark emphasis with triple asterisks, and
nothing ever converted it. 362 of them were rendering to readers across 38
pages - 132 on the register alone - so the archive was showing its own working
notation as if it were prose. site/src/lib/text.js now converts at render time
(escaping first, so data can never inject markup), applied across register,
people, gaps, timeline, errands, corrections, photograph-these, changes and
sources, and stripped from the search index where the text is plain.
THREE GUARDS, so none of this recurs:
- check-links.py fails if an emphasis marker ever reaches a rendered page.
- check-links.py fails if a container class (.prose, .grid, .scroll, .cols2)
  is put on a leaf element - the exact mistake behind yesterday's flex bug.
  Both were verified by deliberately breaking a built page: 2 failures, exit 1.
- The deploy workflow now runs check-links.py before uploading. `astro build`
  exits 0 even when a page throws while rendering - it did today, leaving
  eight pages missing and 3,433 dead links, and reported success. The deploy
  is now gated on the link check rather than on the build's own exit code.

commits.subject: Test WikiTree as a source: zero Lerena, and fix a CSS bug it exposed
commits.body:
WikiTree had never been mentioned anywhere in this archive - not in data/, not in notes/, not on the site - though the archive already leans on Geneanet, Geni, MyHeritage, findmypast and the FamilySearch Tree. A real gap, so it was tested rather than assumed. WikiTree holds ZERO Lerena profiles. Run twice, the second time with variant-matching off so the null could not be the site widening the spelling. That null is worth more than the usual one: WikiTree is a single shared public tree, not millions of private ones, so absence is a measurement rather than a view. LLERENA gives 26 profiles, all Mexican, Cuban-Floridian or Peruvian, plus one Cadiz man of Sancho's generation with no stated link. Not one Uruguayan or Argentine profile of either spelling. So the English side was tested instead, where a hit was actually likely and where this archive is weakest in independence: almost every fact on the Taylor line traces to a single MyHeritage tree. Nearest thing to a hit: two Taylors of Worlingworth, b. 1840 and 1841, William Taylor's own parish - plausibly his sisters. All three Worlingworth profiles were opened; every one has unknown parents. The Devon Brayleys are there in quantity and none connects. The one true Brayley of the right year turned out to be a Queensland Yelland. Recorded as SECONDARY, with Geneanet, Geni and the FamilySearch Tree, and published as a closed source - a source tested and found empty saves the next person an afternoon. Fixes a CSS bug found while checking the new section renders. .prose is a container style (display:flex, column, gap) meant for a
wrapping paragraphs; it had also been applied to 21 individual

elements. A flex container blockifies its children, so every and directly inside those paragraphs was thrown onto its own full-width line - about 27 phrases across six pages reading as fragments instead of sentences. One rule, p.prose{display:block}, fixes all of them and keeps the 80ch measure. Also drops a hardcoded "seven thousand words" from the /searched/ dek; the page is at 9,120 and such counts have gone stale here before.

commits.subject: The site was still publishing a claim I retracted this afternoon
commits.body:
The corrections page has said since 8 September that nothing here is quietly
edited away, and that where a page once said something different it now says the
corrected thing AND says it used to say something else.
The hypotheses page was failing that on its own terms. Its base-rate table still
listed FOUR branches including "Arturo Lerena and Amalia Diaz, born Montevideo
1858, son of Avelino Lerena and Ambrosia Traibel" - the row I withdrew this
afternoon as a conflation of two men, corrected in the data file and on the
corrections page, and never removed from the page that actually publishes it.
Fixed properly rather than silently: the row is gone, the count is three, the
provinces are corrected to Entre Rios, Misiones and Buenos Aires, and a note
underneath says what the table used to say, why it was wrong, and links to the
correction. Which is what the house rule requires.
Also two deks reworded. I wrote "Twelve sections" and "Twelve propositions" this
afternoon; both were accurate, and both were numbers that cannot be derived from
anything and would drift the moment a section was added. They no longer state a
count. Stating a number you cannot derive is how the front page came to claim
129 people when there were 138.
And the people index said "Five are connected to the direct line" when fourteen
are. It now derives all three figures - connected, excluded, unplaced - from the
data.

commits.subject: Three pages scrolled sideways on a phone, and one of them was my doing
commits.body:
Tested every page at 375px by loading each into a 375px iframe and measuring
scrollWidth against clientWidth - rather than spot-checking two and assuming.
Three failed.
/errands/ scrolled 412 PIXELS. The cause was mine, from this afternoon: the
errand handing David three FamilySearch searches carries a 150-character URL,
and a URL has nothing to break on. Body prose now sets overflow-wrap:anywhere,
so a long token wraps instead of widening the page. It is the right default for
an archive that quotes film numbers, arks and search URLs constantly.
/roadmap/ and /photograph-these/ each scrolled about 32px, from the labelled
rule. Its .lb label was flex:0 0 auto - unshrinkable - so a long label pushed
the row wider than the screen. It may now shrink and wrap, with tighter spacing
and letter-spacing below 620px.
Also in this commit: contents lists for /argentina/ (12 sections), /taylor/ (9)
and /name/ (7), on the same pattern and under the same build check as searched,
hypotheses and corrections. Every reading page over about 1,700 words now has a
way in.

commits.subject: Phase 4: close the ring
commits.body:
Part of standardising the seven family archives. Until now they barely
acknowledged each other: D'Arcy linked to five siblings, Mazza to two,
Falco and Blazevic to one each, and Booyzen and Defranceschi — the one
every other archive points at — linked to nobody at all. A reader landing
on one had no way to learn the other six existed.
One src/data/archives.json, identical in all seven, holding each archive's
name, address, accent, where it comes from, one line of what it is, and the
surnames it covers. One SiblingArchives component renders every entry
except the one you are standing in, working out which that is from
BASE_URL, so no per-site configuration can drift. It sits in the footer, so
it is on every page of every archive.
Each card wears its own archive's colour, which is the payoff of Phase 1:
seven distinguishable accents mean the ring reads as seven places rather
than one list.
Two things fixed on the way:
Falco's dark accent was still the teal every archive shipped before Phase 1,
so in dark mode it was indistinguishable from Defranceschi. It takes
#E0836A, 5.92:1 on its own dark panel. That completes the colour work: all
seven are now distinct in both themes, not just in light.
The ring was painting light-theme hexes onto a dark ground. The component
now publishes both a light and a dark value and lets the stylesheet choose —
set from CSS rather than inline, because an inline custom property would
have beaten the media query.

commits.subject: Six of today's corrections were malformed, and light mode is what showed it
commits.body:
Two jobs, and the first was found only by looking at the site on paper-white for
the first time today. Everything I had checked until now rendered dark, because
the preview pane follows the app theme.
THE CORRECTIONS PAGE HAD SIX ENTRIES WITH EMPTY FIELDS. data/corrections.tsv
carries five columns - date, severity, what was said, what is true, how it was
caught - and every entry I added today had THREE. So my title landed in the
severity column, my body in "It said", and "It is:" and "Caught by:" rendered
blank. Six of the twenty entries on the page the archive's honesty rests on were
broken, and the serious/minor tallies in the header counted none of them.
All six rewritten into the proper schema. Four are graded serious - the LERINA
exclusion reasoning, the two Arturo Lerenas, the one-way parent edges, and the
duplicate register names - and two minor. Every one now says how it was caught,
which is the transferable part and the reason the column exists.
AND THE PAGE ITSELF. Twenty entries rendered as one undifferentiated run of
panels. Now grouped by the day they were caught, each day a labelled rule with a
hidden linkable heading, and a contents list at the top giving each day's count
and how many of them were serious. Same idiom as the changelog, same build check
enforcing that no day can go unlisted.
Light mode itself is fine - the violet accent the standardisation commit
introduced reads well on the paper ground, and nothing else was amiss. But I had
approved a palette I had never seen, and that was worth correcting.
198 pages, 257 ids, 0 broken.

commits.subject: Two more notes brought up to what the acts now say
commits.body:
Continuing the sweep for register notes that went stale this afternoon.
GILBERTO LERENA still read only "No proven link to Pablo Armando" - true, and
worth keeping - but said nothing of what was learned today: his father is
documented rather than asserted, because his brother's marriage act of 1864
names their parents. It now also states the coincidence plainly, that a Lerena
at the centre of Argentine breeding sits beside a Pablo Armando who trained and
owned racehorses, while keeping the brotherhood itself marked secondary, since
that still rests on published genealogy and not an act.
JUSTINIANA LENGUAS GONZALEZ was described from the trees. She is named in TWO
acts read here - her son's marriage of 1864, at which she was a witness, and her
granddaughter's baptism of 1869, which calls her one of the abuelos paternos.
Her note now leads with those and keeps only her own parentage as secondary. It
also carries the thing that makes the family legible: her sister Sixta married
Candido Juanico, so the Lenguas married into both houses, and Sixta stood
godmother to the 1869 child.

commits.subject: Two register notes were still calling documented facts unverified
commits.body:
Looking at a person page on a phone turned up a content fault, not a layout one.
Don Luis Eugenio Lerena Lenguas's note still read:
  Published Uruguayan genealogy makes him a son of Luis Lerena y Fernandez and
  Justiniana Lenguas Gonzalez ... That parentage is SECONDARY and unverified.
It has not been unverified since this morning. The Montevideo marriage act of 19
December 1864 names him "hijo legitimo de Don Luis y de Dona Justiniana
Lenguas", and his daughter Laura Adela's baptism of 1869 names the same two as
her paternal grandparents - two acts, independently. The page was contradicting
its own archive.
The godfather's row carried the same stale sentence and has been rewritten too.
Both now separate the two claims properly: the PARENTAGE is documented; what
stays SECONDARY is only the equation of that "Don Luis" with the Luis Lerena y
Fernandez (1811-1878) of the published trees, and through him the line up to
Sancho. That distinction is the whole point of the tiering and it had been lost
in a note nobody re-read.
Also recorded there now: five children on primary records, and his death dated
to before 11 July 1910 by his widow's registration.

commits.subject: The contents lists I added today were unreadable on a phone
commits.body:
Checked the site at 375px for the first time - something I had not done at all
today - and the three contents lists added this afternoon were still in two
columns, each about 110px wide, breaking every entry across three or four lines.
They were written with an inline style="columns:2", and an inline style cannot
carry a media query. Moved to a .cols2 class that drops to one column below
620px, with break-inside:avoid so an entry cannot be split across the fold.
Applied to all three - searched, hypotheses, changes.

commits.subject: Fingerprint the stylesheet, because a cached one had been quietly lying
commits.body:
Scrolling the deployed changelog to check the new fold-away entries showed the
day's date TWICE - once in the labelled rule, once as a large heading beneath it
- although the markup carried class="vh" and the stylesheet carried the rule
that hides it.
The markup was right and the CSS was right. The BROWSER was serving a cached
styles.css from before that class existed. Which means every returning visitor
to this site has been laid out by whatever version of the stylesheet their
browser happened to keep - and would have been, for as long as it kept it.
The stylesheet is now fingerprinted with a short SHA-1 of its own contents:
styles.css?v=fa62f94e. The URL changes exactly when the file changes and never
otherwise, so a CSS change reaches everybody on their next visit and nobody
re-downloads it for nothing.
AND THE CHECKER CAUGHT ITS OWN REGRESSION. Adding the query string broke all 198
pages in tools/check-links.py, which tested whether a path ENDED in .css and now
saw "styles.css?v=fa62f94e". That is the checker doing its job on the first
change after it was written: it fails loudly rather than passing quietly. It now
strips the query before testing the path.
198 pages, 251 ids, 0 broken.

commits.subject: Phase 1: own accent, and trailing slashes
commits.body:
Part of standardising the seven family archives. No content touched.
This was the third archive wearing the Defranceschi palette — the same
#1F5C6B teal as Defranceschi and Blazevic, light and dark. Takes violet
#5B3A96, with #B49AE8 for dark; 7.8:1 on paper, 7.44:1 on the dark ground.
Violet rather than the amber the children's site uses for this line: the
Mazza archive has just taken ochre, and amber beside ochre is not a
distinction anyone would make at a glance. Where alignment with the
children's palette costs legibility, legibility wins.
Trailing slashes: this was the only archive mixing both styles — 82 links
with, 64 without. Now all 146 have one.
Verified: 198 pages built, 14,357 internal links crawled, all resolve.

commits.subject: A contents list for the hypotheses page too, and a count got checked before it was published
commits.body:
Hypotheses had grown to 5,250 words across thirteen sections with no way in -
the same fault as the searched page, and the second-longest reading page on the
site.
Every h2 now carries a stable id and the page opens with a list of the
propositions, enforced by the same build check: a proposition cannot be added or
renamed without appearing in the list.
The first draft of the dek said "Thirteen of them". There are thirteen HEADINGS
but only TWELVE PROPOSITIONS - the thirteenth is the Retired section, which is
where hypotheses go when they are disproved, not a hypothesis. It now reads
"Twelve propositions ... and a last section for the ones already retired", which
is what is actually on the page. Small, but this is the second count today that
would have been wrong if it had not been read back.
198 pages, 251 ids, 0 broken.

commits.subject: Make the changelog navigable, and say what it leaves out
commits.body:
The changelog had become the largest page on the site - THIRTY-THREE THOUSAND
WORDS - with no headings, no way in, and every commit body expanded. It is the
archive's best feature and its least usable page.
THREE CHANGES.
Days are now real headings with stable ids, and the page opens with a list of
them and their change counts. The headings are visually hidden - each day
already carries a labelled rule above it - but they exist for linking and for
screen readers, and the anchor checker written an hour ago enforces that every
one of them appears in the contents list.
Each entry's REASONING is folded behind a "Why" disclosure. The subject line
stays visible, so the page can be scanned; the argument is one click away. No
JavaScript - a details element and eight lines of CSS.
And thirty-two commits are OMITTED: those whose entire subject is "Rebuild the
changelog". They are the mechanical consequence of the commit before them and
contain no reasoning at all. But they are COUNTED AND DECLARED in the page's own
prose, with a link to the full commit list in the repository, because an archive
that quietly shortens its own log is doing the exact opposite of what the log is
for. The builder carries a comment saying so, so the next person to touch it
knows the rule was deliberate.
116 changes across 4 days, plus 32 mechanical rebuilds named as such.
198 pages, 237 ids, 0 broken.

commits.subject: Give the longest page a contents list the build enforces, and promote the checker
commits.body:
THE SEARCHED PAGE HAD GROWN TO 22 SECTIONS AND 7,700 WORDS with no way into it,
and two of those sections were both called "The register itself" - one the first
pass of 10 September, one the 750-act sweep of the 13th - sitting four sections
apart with the later one first. Renamed so the relationship reads:
  The register itself - carried to 750 acts, and the index vindicated
  The register itself - where that read began
Every h2 now carries a stable id derived from its own text, and the page opens
with a contents list.
AND THE LIST MAKES A PROMISE THE BUILD KEEPS. The first draft of that block said
the list "is generated from the headings themselves, so it cannot drift" - which
was FALSE as written: it was generated once by a script, not at build time. An
archive that publishes an untrue sentence about its own machinery is worse than
one with no contents list. So the machinery was made to match the claim rather
than the claim softened to match the machinery.
tools/check-links.py - promoted out of the ad-hoc heredoc I had been pasting
after every build, and extended. It now:
  - validates in-page #anchors, not just pages and assets
  - treats any page carrying an id="contents" as making a promise, and checks
    that EVERY h2 on that page is linked from within it
Both directions were tested by breaking the built HTML deliberately: renaming
one heading produced two failures - a contents link pointing at a section that
no longer exists, and a section missing from the contents list - and a non-zero
exit. The page's sentence now reads "the build checks this list against the
page", which is true.
198 pages, 232 ids, 0 broken.

commits.subject: Two more hardcoded counts, and close the loop on a prediction the site made
commits.body:
"Eight numbers" on the front page, when today's work had made it ten. Now
derived from the array, spelled out, so it cannot drift again - the same fault
as the 129/138 register count an hour ago, and the third instance today of a
figure typed by hand in an archive whose whole method is generating pages from
the data.
AND A LOOP CLOSED. The Argentina page has carried this since 8 September, under
"Uruguay is not a detour":
  Stated plainly so it is not forgotten later: if the Argentine search stalls,
  the correct next move is Uruguay, not a harder Argentine search.
The Argentine search did stall, and the instruction was followed. The page now
says what came of it: one Lerena in a hundred and seventy years of the Rosario
index, and the act behind her saying "naturales del E. Oriental"; the full-text
measurement, where LERENA runs 6.4x commoner in Uruguay while its twin LLERENA
runs 3.6x the other way and two reference surnames both favour Argentina; and
the thing it has NOT produced, which is Juan Carlos.
It seemed worth marking where a page told its own future what to do and turned
out to be right.

commits.subject: Lead the front page with what the day actually found
commits.body:
The banner still led with 10 September - "His father has a name" - which was the
right lead for three days and stopped being it. The front page is the most
prominent editorial judgement on the site and it was out of date.
New lead, 13 September: THEY WERE NOT A ROSARIO FAMILY. Both volumes of the
baptism index read end to end, 1731 to 1901; the surname appears once in a
hundred and seventy years; the act behind that one entry says of both parents
"naturales del E. Oriental". No baptism for Pablo Armando, none for his father,
no Lerena marriage 1867-1885, not one Lerena in the 1895 census of Santa Fe -
and then the register itself read act by act, 750 consecutive baptisms, to test
whether the 1945 index could be trusted. It agrees everywhere.
A household that lives in a parish leaves baptisms. This one leaves nothing,
which is no longer a gap in the searching but a fact about the family.
With a footnote for the death index and its missing L section, 1840-1881.
The enrolment card keeps its panel directly beneath, under "Before that", in the
quieter rule colour. It is still the best document in the archive; it is no
longer the news.

commits.subject: Record the block, and hand three searches to David
commits.body:
FamilySearch is up - in an ordinary browser. It is not up for THIS session:
every request from the automated browser pane is refused on contact by Incapsula,
ark pages included, which makes it a block on this client rather than a rate
limit that can be paced around. Four separate blocks today, all earned by the
day's reading rate, and this one does not lift on the timescale the others did.
Rather than keep poking at it - which lengthens these things - the three
searches that would each close an open question are written up as an errand with
the URLs in full, so they take about two minutes in a normal browser:
  1. Luis Eugenio Lerena's death, narrowed to between 1880 and July 1910
  2. Julia Juanico's baptism, born Montevideo about 1844
  3. Candido Juanico's first marriage to Juliana Gonzalez, which is currently
     inference from dates and not a document
Paste anything back and I will read the images, which is the part that needs me.

commits.subject: Roadmap route 1 rewritten - Montevideo went from a plan to a household
commits.body:
Route 1 still read "worked once, and the indexes came back empty", which was
true this morning and stopped being true by the afternoon. It now says what
actually happened: the one documented Lerena household of that generation in the
River Plate is open from the marriage act of December 1864 to Julia Juanico's
death in July 1910, with five children, every member on a primary record, and
Laura Adela's baptism naming every grandparent in a single line.
And it says the thing that matters: Juan Carlos Lerena is not among them, and
not in the indexed Uruguayan record either.
What is still open is listed precisely - Luis Eugenio's own death, now narrowed
to 1880-1910; Julia's baptism; Candido Juanico's first marriage to Juliana
Gonzalez, which is inference from dates and not a document; and the reading full
text cannot do for you, the Montevideo marriage registers of the 1870s.

commits.subject: Julia Juanico's death, and the date it puts on her husband's
commits.body:
Montevideo, civil registration certificate No. 357 of 1910, image ark
3:1:3Q9M-CS2W-K9BG-8, read at tile level 12:
  En Montevideo, el dia doce de Julio de mil novecientos diez, a las once de la
  manana ... declarando que a las cuatro de la tarde del dia de ayer, y en la
  calle Constituyente No. 992, ha fallecido JULIA JUANICO DE LERENA, del sexo
  femenino, de nacionalidad oriental, nacida en esta ciudad, de SESENTA Y SEIS
  ANOS DE EDAD, DE ESTADO VIUDA, y de profesion labores del sexo.
Declared by two clerks - Don Antonio Vicaria of calle Nicaragua 139 and Don
Lorenzo Nicolas Baca - before the Juez de Paz of the fifteenth section.
She died on 11 July 1910, aged sixty-six, born in Montevideo about 1844, which
makes her about twenty at her marriage in December 1864. Nothing in the
household needs stretching to fit.
AND SHE WAS A WIDOW. So Luis Eugenio Lerena Lenguas died BEFORE 11 JULY 1910 -
somewhere between 1880, when their last child was born, and that summer. That
squares with their son Enrique's registration of May 1914, which calls both
parents fallecidos.
His own death record is not found. The search for it was cut short when
FamilySearch firewalled this session for the third time today - all three my
doing, not theirs. The errand carries the exact window and the two searches to
run when the block lifts.
198 pages, 0 broken links.

commits.subject: Laura Adela - a fifth child, and one act that names every grandparent
commits.body:
Looking for the DEATHS of Luis Lerena Lenguas and Julia Juanico turned up
something better than what I went for.
A CIVIL TRANSCRIPTION of March 1902 - Luis Cincinato Bollo, Director General del
Registro del Estado Civil, certifying an old parish act into the civil register
under the Uruguayan law of 9 July 1888. Entry No. 51, "Lerena, Laura Adela",
image ark 3:1:3Q9M-CS2W-XSMB-7, read at tile level 12. The priest attests that in
libro treinta y cuatro de Bautismos, folio doscientos setenta y uno, stands this:
  En tres de Marzo del ano de mil ochocientos sesenta y nueve el Presbitero Don
  Jose Miralda, con licencia del infrascripto Cura Rector de esta Iglesia Matriz
  de Montevideo, bautice solemnemente en ella a LAURA ADELA, que nacio el veinte
  y siete de Junio del ano anterior, hija legitima de DON LUIS EUGENIO LERENA y
  de Da JULIA JUANICO, orientales. ABUELOS PATERNOS DON LUIS Y Da JUSTINIANA
  LENGUAS; MATERNOS Dn CANDIDO Y Da JULIANA GONZALEZ. Padrinos Don Candido
  Juanico y Da Sixta Lenguas.
THREE THINGS AT ONCE.
A FIFTH CHILD. Laura Adela, born 27 June 1868, baptised 3 March 1869 - slotting
neatly between Maria Julia (1865) and Luis (1872).
HIS FULL NAME. "Don LUIS EUGENIO Lerena", which no other record had given. The
register, the relations and the charts now carry it.
BOTH SETS OF GRANDPARENTS, IN ONE LINE, IN A PARISH ACT. Everything this archive
had inferred or taken from a tree about the generation above Luis Lerena Lenguas
is simply stated here - his father Luis, his mother Justiniana Lenguas; her
father Candido, her mother Juliana Gonzalez - independently of the marriage act
of 1864 and agreeing with it exactly.
AND THE GODMOTHER IS THE KNOT. The godparents are Don Candido Juanico, the
baby's maternal grandfather, and Dona Sixta Lenguas, whom he married in 1857 -
and Sixta Lenguas Gonzalez is the SISTER of Justiniana Lenguas Gonzalez, the
baby's paternal grandmother. So the child's two godparents are her mother's
father and her father's mother's sister, who are married to each other. The
Lenguas married into both houses, which is why the two surnames keep appearing
together and why a SIXTA turns up among the children a decade later.
Luis Eugenio Lerena Lenguas and Julia Juanico now show five children each on
their charts.
AND STILL NOTHING TOUCHES PABLO ARMANDO LERENA.
198 pages, 0 broken links.

commits.subject: Record why the CEMLA manifests cannot be opened from here
commits.body:
Tried CEMLA for the four LERINA arrivals of 1889, whose exclusion was narrowed

iframe at search.cemla.com and is gated by a CAPTCHA - field "CaptchaCode" -

Worth saying plainly for whoever picks it up: on the evidence of its own

closable online by anyone. It is on the gaps page in those terms, so that a
future reader does not mistake an index row for a document - which is the error
this archive has had to correct twice already.

commits.subject: Derive the front-page count instead of typing it, and add the gap to the figures
commits.body:

shorten as the day's reading accumulates. So: offline work.
THE FRONT PAGE SAID 129 PEOPLE IN THE REGISTER. There are 138. A hand-typed
count, correct when written and stale within days - the register grew by nine

from the TSVs so that page and data cannot drift; this one figure had escaped

AND A NEW FIGURE, because it is one of the more striking things the archive now
knows:
  1840-1881 - the years for which the Rosario death index has no L section at
  all; the book runs A to F and stops.
Checked the other hardcoded numbers while I was there. "2,124 people bear this
surname in the whole world" on the horses and name pages is the global count of
the surname, not an internal tally, and is correct. The "entries" figures on the
searched page are descriptive prose about the index sections, not counts of

commits.subject: Take Sancho out of the tree and put him in the records
commits.body:
Everything this archive said about Sancho Llerena rested on the FAMILYSEARCH
TREE - a user's decision that fourteen sources were one man, and vitals with no
citation attached. That is precisely the kind of evidence this archive has been
caught by before, so it was checked.
Not by working through the tree's own source list, but by going at the INDEXED
RECORDS directly: given name Sancho, surname Llerena or Lerena, country Uruguay.
THE CENSUS. Uruguay, Census Records 1726-1858, index ark 1:1:61LW-R54J:
  Sancho Llerena. Sexo masculino. Age 45 years. BIRTHPLACE: ANDALUZIA.
And the image was opened - ark 3:1:3QS7-99ZR-NKNR. It carries a filmer's
warning, "Paginas Rotas - Escritura poco Legible", and it is very faint. It is
legible all the same. Household No. 59, CALLE SAN JUAN, MONTEVIDEO, and the
entry reads:
  Sancho Llerena
  Maria Fernandez
Husband and wife, one line under the other, in the record itself.
THE SIX OTHERS, all Uruguayan, all naming the same wife and the same children:
  Sancho Llerena    father of the bride; child Justa Pastora Llerena
  Sancho Lerena     child Avelino Lerena
  D. Sancho Lerena  child Dominga Lorena
  Sancho Llerena    child Dominga Llarena
  Sancio Llerena    child Dominga Josefa
  Sancho Lorena     father of the groom; child rendered "Avelino Serena"
WHAT THAT SETTLES. The alternation is NOT a tree user's idea. The records
themselves spell the man Llerena, Lerena, Sancio Llerena, D. Sancho Lerena and
Lorena, and his children Llarena and Serena. And a census gives his birthplace
in one word: Andaluzia.
WHAT IT STILL DOES NOT SETTLE, and both are on the page. That these are all ONE
MAN remains an inference - a strong one, resting on the repeated wife and
children in one city, but an inference, and the fourteen parish acts behind the
tree's list have still not been opened one by one. And CORDOBA specifically, as
against Andalusia generally, still comes only from the tree: the census gives
the province, not the town.
Nothing here touches Pablo Armando Lerena.

commits.subject: Make every register row addressable, then draw the households that were already documented
commits.body:
FamilySearch firewalled this session again partway through - my own reading rate,
as before - so the network-dependent items were set aside and the offline ones
done instead.
FIRST, A FAULT FOUND BEFORE IT DID ANY DAMAGE. The people builder looks people up
with a plain dictionary keyed on NAME. Eleven names appeared twice or three times
in the register - three Francisco Lerenas, three Jose Llerenas, two Carlos
Lerenas, two Gilbertos, two Avelino Carloses, two Juan Larenas, two Maria
Larenas, two Antonio Larenas - so the later row silently won and THIRTEEN ROWS
COULD NOT BE ADDRESSED BY NAME AT ALL. Slugs had been disambiguated; names never
were.
Nothing was visibly wrong, because no relationship edge happened to name an
ambiguous person. But I was about to add twenty-four edges, several of them to a
"Carlos LERENA" and a "Gilberto LERENA", and they would have attached to the
wrong man in silence.
Every duplicate now carries a short factual tag - "Carlos LERENA (b.1885, arr.
1926)" against "Carlos LERENA (b.1884, Retiro baptism)" - and the builder now
REFUSES TO BUILD if two rows share a name, printing the offenders. On the
corrections page.
THEN THE EDGES. Twenty-four relationships this archive had already READ and
recorded in its register notes, and simply never drew:
  Gilberto Lerena and Julia Salvanach and their seven children in the 1895
  Buenos Aires census; Carlos Lerena of the Retiro baptism, his parents, both his
  wives and his son Avelino Carlos of the Mendoza baptism; Pedro Llerena and
  Sofia Clavijo and their daughter Susana; Francisco Llerena and Rafaela Daraz
  and their son Baldomero and his wife Margarita Correas; the Carlos and Rosa
  who crossed together in 1926; and the two Gilbertos, father and son, who
  crossed together on the CAP. NORTE in 1928.
People with no relations at all: 110 before, 93 now. Most of the remainder are
genuinely unplaced, which is what unplaced means.
AND AN ERRAND CLOSED WITHOUT NEEDING DAVID. "Gilberto Lerena Lenguas - his
parents and siblings" had been sitting behind a Geneanet CAPTCHA. His brother's
marriage act of 19 December 1864 names their parents outright, so his parentage
is now documented from a primary record. The siblings remain secondary.
Plus an audit of all 138 people pages after yesterday's chart change: charts
present wherever there are relations, absent wherever there are none, no stray
numerals. It did turn up "Of the 1 relationships in the chart above" on three
pages. Fixed.

commits.subject: Open the three Montevideo images - and find the sisters standing in each other's acts
commits.body:
Three records were marked PRIMARY yesterday on the strength of MACHINE
TRANSCRIPTS. By this archive's own rule that is not good enough, and the rule
exists because it was broken once already. All three are now opened.
LUIS, buried 13 December 1897. Catedral de la Inmaculada Concepcion, image ark
3:1:3Q9M-C9B7-LSMR-1. The margin reads "Lerena, Luis":
  di sepultura eclesiastica al cadaver de Luis Lerena, oriental, de veinte y
  cinco anos de edad, soltero e hijo legitimo de Luis Lerena Lenguas y Julia
  Juanico: fallecio ayer.
ENRIQUE, died 16 May 1914. Montevideo civil registration no. 46, image ark
3:1:3Q9M-CS2W-J9WM-2 - a printed form filled in by hand before Cesar Schiaffino,
Oficial del Estado Civil of the sixth section, on the declaration of two clerks,
Hercules Sacchi and Oscar Mendez. Cause of death UREMIA, certified by Dr A.
Mane. And the line that matters:
  el finado era hijo legitimo de Don Luis Lerena Lenguas y de Dona Julia
  Juanico, FALLECIDOS.
Both parents already dead by May 1914 - the first thing this archive knows about
the end of Luis Lerena Lenguas and Julia Juanico.
EMA SIXTA, married 30 June 1913. La Union, act No. 90, page 492, image ark
3:1:3Q9M-C9B7-T7P2-W:
  contrajo Don Jose Pedro Massera ... de cuarenta y seis anos de edad ... con
  Dona Ema Sixta Lerena Joanico ... de treinta y tres anos de edad, hija
  legitima de Don Luis Lerena Lenguas y Dona Julia Joanico, finados. Fueron
  testigos, Don Jaime Herrera y Dona Maria Lerena Joanico de Herrera.
THE WITNESSES ARE HER SISTER AND HER BROTHER-IN-LAW - the couple of the act of
November 1886. Two marriage registers twenty-seven years apart, and the same
people standing in both. That is the kind of internal agreement that tells you a
household has been reconstructed correctly rather than assembled.
AND WHO THE GROOM WAS. Jose Pedro Massera (1866-1942), professor of philosophy
at the Universidad de la Republica from 1887 to 1927 and a Colorado senator from
1927. The age on the act fits his birth year exactly, and independent sources
give his wife as Ema Lerena Joanico and their son as JOSE LUIS MASSERA
(1915-2002), Uruguay's most celebrated mathematician and a political prisoner
under the dictatorship.
So the sister of the only Lerena baptised at Rosario in a hundred and seventy
years married into that family. Recorded because it is true and because it was
reached from an act read here.
IT BEARS NOT AT ALL ON THE CENTRAL QUESTION. Nothing connects this household to
Pablo Armando Lerena or to Juan Carlos, and a striking name must not be allowed
to do the work of evidence. Said in those words in the data file and the note.
One correction folded in: Ema Sixta is thirty-three on the 1913 act, so born
about 1880, where a findmypast index had said 1876.

commits.subject: Wire in the Montevideo household - and find the charts had been half-blind all along
commits.body:
TWO JOBS, and the first uncovered the second.
ONE. The Montevideo household had primary documentation for every member and NOT
ONE RELATION EDGE. Eighteen edges added to data/relations.tsv, each carrying the
act it rests on: the marriage of 19 December 1864; both sets of parents named in
it; all four children; and the two SECONDARY links upward to Sancho Llerena and
across to Gilberto, marked "tree" so the chart says so. Two people added to the
register - Dona Justiniana Lenguas Gonzalez and Sancho Llerena Aguilar.
TWO, AND IT AFFECTS EVERY PAGE IN THE ARCHIVE. The charts read relations.tsv,
where a link is written once - "X, father, Y". The builder recorded that on X's
page and NEVER REVERSED IT onto Y's. So every parent here showed an EMPTY
CHILDREN LIST unless somebody had also written an explicit "child" row. Thirty-
eight parent edges were being read one way; there were only fifteen explicit
child rows to compensate.
Pablo Armando, Juan Carlos, Maria Lerena, Mary Septima Taylor, Roque, Roseline
Forbes and Doreen Chappell all had children in the data and none on their
charts. They have them now.
Fixing it immediately exposed a second fault. This register deliberately keeps a
row for the mangled machine-index reading of a person it has already resolved -
"ARMAND[O] LORENA (as machine-indexed) = Pablo Armando LERENA" - and that row
carries its own parent edges, correctly. Reversed, it made Juan Carlos and Maria
appear to have TWO children where they have one. The builder now reads the
"= <name>" convention as an ALIAS and neither counts it as a child nor as a
sibling. The matching allows for the canonical row carrying a parenthetical,
which is why the first attempt at it silently did nothing.
Both faults are on the corrections page. Verified by reading the built HTML
rather than trusting the build: Don Luis Lerena Lenguas now shows two parents, a
wife, four children and a sibling; Juan Carlos and Maria show one child each.
196 pages, 0 broken links.

commits.subject: Sweep Buenos Aires - find nothing, and measure something better instead
commits.body:
Item 5 was the Buenos Aires parish registers through full text, looking for a
Lerena marrying a Maria between 1870 and 1882. Buenos Aires IS in the full-text
corpus; Santa Fe is not.
Nothing. The Argentine Lerenas in the corpus are twentieth-century, or colonial
Buenos Aires probate officials - a Ramon Lerena, Alcalde, in 1800. The Montevideo
"Carlos Lerena" hits turn out to be Carlos A. Lerena, the Traibel branch,
standing godfather at Cordon in 1878. No Juan Carlos, no Maria.
But the search produced something better than it was looking for. The two
spellings can be COUNTED. The full-text Place filter gives per-country totals,
and anyone can repeat this in two minutes:
                      Argentina    Uruguay
  LERENA                    701      4,517   Uruguay 6.4x Argentina
  LLERENA                 3,415        947   Argentina 3.6x Uruguay
  Fernandez (reference) 608,205    305,473   Argentina 2.0x Uruguay
  Bustamante (reference) 75,647      9,328   Argentina 8.1x Uruguay
A control is necessary because the two national corpora are not the same size
and every surname has its own geography - so the comparison is made against TWO
REFERENCE SURNAMES measured the same way, rather than against an assumed corpus
ratio.
Both references run Argentina-heavy, one by twice and one by eight times. So
does LLERENA. LERENA is the only one of the four that reverses, and it reverses
hard - six times more common in Uruguay than in Argentina.
And it is the spelling this family used.
It also sits neatly with Sancho Llerena Aguilar: a LLERENA of Cordoba marries at
Canelones in 1791, his descendants are written both ways in the Uruguayan
registers for forty years, and today the single-l form is the Uruguayan one
while the double-l form stayed Argentine.
WHAT IT DOES NOT SAY, on the page in as many words: this measures a DIGITISED
CORPUS, not a population. Coverage is uneven between countries and periods and
the handwriting recognition misreads. It is evidence about where the NAME lives,
not about where any particular family lived, and it cannot place Juan Carlos
Lerena anywhere at all.
194 pages, 0 broken links.

commits.subject: Open the Montevideo household from the marriage act to the last burial
commits.body:
Full text was given the phrase "Lerena Lenguas". Seven hits in the entire
corpus, all Montevideo, and between them they open the whole household.
THE MARRIAGE - San Francisco de Asis, Ciudad Vieja, act No. 258, read from the
image rather than the transcript:
  En diez y nueve de Diciembre de mil ochocientos sesenta y cuatro ... el
  matrimonio que por palabras de presente contrajo Don Luis Lerena y Lenguas,
  natural de esta Republica, soltero, e hijo legitimo de Don Luis y de Dona
  Justiniana Lenguas, con Dona Julia Juanico, del propio estado y vecindad, e
  hija legitima del Sr. Don Candido y de Dona Juliana Gonzalez; fueron testigos
  el Dr. Don Candido Juanico y Dona Justiniana Len[guas].
That is the join the whole Montevideo argument rested on, and this morning it
rested on a TREE. Geneanet and the FamilySearch Tree both asserted that Luis
Lerena Lenguas was a son of Luis Lerena y Fernandez and Justiniana Lenguas
Gonzalez, and neither cited anything checkable. The act states it. The
generation above him is no longer secondary.
It also names Julia Juanico's parents for the first time: Dr Don Candido Juanico
- abogado, magistrado, legislador y hombre politico, son of Francisco Juanico
and Juliana Texeira - who stood as a witness at his own daughter's wedding, and
Dona Juliana Gonzalez. Published genealogy has Candido marrying SIXTA Lenguas
Gonzalez in 1857, too late for a daughter marrying in 1864, so Julia belongs to
an earlier marriage. That step is inference from dates and is marked as such.
And the date fits without strain: married 19 December 1864, first child born at
Rosario 8 October 1865.
THE CHILDREN - all four, from primary records:
  Maria Julia Margarita Josefa Emirena Justiniana - b. ROSARIO 8 Oct 1865,
    m. Jaime Herrera, Montevideo, 1886
  Luis - b. c.1872, d. Montevideo 12 Dec 1897, aged 25, unmarried
  Enrique Lerena Juanico - b. Montevideo c.1873, d. Montevideo 16 May 1914,
    aged 41, unmarried, an empleado, at Plaza Libertad 1143
  Ema Sixta - b. 1876, m. Don Jose Pedro Marsera, La Union, Montevideo, 1913
Ema Sixta is the "Emma Liseta, 1876, father Luis, mother Julia" copied from a
findmypast index on 9 September and left unremarked - four days before anyone
knew whose daughter she was. And the name SIXTA is her mother's stepmother's:
the family names children off both sides of itself, which is what a real
household does.
AND THE POINT OF THE EXERCISE. JUAN CARLOS LERENA IS NOT AMONG THEM. The one
Lerena family documented in the River Plate in this generation has now been
opened from the marriage to the last burial, and he is not in it.
That is a clean negative and it costs hypothesis 1c nothing - it never claimed
Pablo Armando descended from THIS household, only that the surname's River Plate
home is Montevideo. What has changed is that the household is fully mapped, so
nobody has to wonder about it again.
Two errands closed. 194 pages, 0 broken links.

commits.subject: Carry the 1882 register into the next volume, acts 851-914
commits.body:
The waypoint "Bautismos 1882-1883" overlaps the last one: it opens at act 851
where the previous volume ran to 862. Six acts to an opening here rather than

Acts 851 to 914 read - 23 July to 2 August 1882. No Lerena. One L-surname

Resume point recorded exactly: image 12, ark S3HT-XS7G-BS, act 915.
And a note on priority, written into the data file so the decision is visible
rather than silent. The POINT of reading the register act by act was to test
whether the 1945 typescript index is complete. That test is done and passed
across 750 consecutive acts, February to July 1882: wherever the index says

commits.subject: Open the Rosario death index - the biggest untried thing in the city
commits.body:
Every Rosario sweep in this archive had been for baptisms and marriages. Nobody
had opened the DEATHS. And a death act does the same work as a baptism act: it
names the parents of the deceased. If Juan Carlos or Maria Lerena died at
Rosario, the death index is where they would be, and it would name THEIR
parents - pushing the line back a generation in a single entry.
"Indice de defunciones 1800-1888", eighty-six images, HANDWRITTEN - not the 1945
typescript that indexes the baptisms. Four columns to a page, surname / given
name / folio, grouped by letter and then by libro and year.
And it is not one index. It is a composite, bound together:
  images 3-44   Death index, first sequence: A-Z, 1800-1839
  images 45-53  Death index, second sequence: "Letra A" to "Letra S", 1882-1888
  images ~51-55 An index whose entries read "X CON Y" - marriages, not deaths
  images 56-58  "Bautismos de los Yndios" - indigenous baptisms, letters A-P
  images 59-86  Death index, third sequence: c.1838-1869, AND IT STOPS AT F
BOTH L SECTIONS THAT EXIST WERE READ IN FULL, AND NEITHER HOLDS A LERENA.
1800-1839, images 27-29: Lencinas, Leguizamon, Lopez, Ludueña, Lucena, Leon,
Lujan, Llanos, Lescano, Lavallen, Lozano, Lemos, Luna, Lira, Luque, Loza, Lazo,
Latorre, Lagos, Livia, Lumbre, Larrea, Langüines - hundreds of them. One near
miss logged: LOVERRA, Maria (1820), Lov- and not Ler-.
1882-1888, image 48: seventy-odd entries across seven years, including the year
of his birth. Lugones, Ludueña, Lobos, Luria, Ledesma, Lucero, Leguizamon, Loza,
Lescano, Lunas, Lemos, Limbo, Lejarza, Lazarte, Leahy, Lopez, Llanes, Leon,
Lazo, Lezcano, Lencina, Lavallen, Labao, Losarto, Lubes.
AND THEN THE BOOK RUNS OUT. The third sequence - the one that would cover
roughly 1840 to 1881 - runs A, B, C, D, E, F, and the volume ends mid-alphabet.
THERE IS NO L SECTION FOR THOSE YEARS IN THIS FILM.
That is not a gap in the searching. It is a gap in the record, and it falls
exactly where it hurts most: a man and a woman who had a son at Rosario in
February 1882 are most likely to have died in the decades either side of it, and
for the four decades before it the finding aid simply does not exist. It is now
on the gaps page as something this archive CANNOT close, as distinct from
something it has not tried.
What remains: the death REGISTERS survive to 1875 and are filmed, so a Rosario
death between 1841 and 1875 is still findable - act by act, the way the 1882
baptism register was read. Far larger than an index would have been, and now the
only route. After 1875 the collection holds no death register at all.
METHOD NOTE worth keeping: level 13 drops tiles on this film - eleven of a
hundred and eighty-seven on one page-half, in regular horizontal bands, after
ten retry passes. Level 12 at 0.58 scale, one page-half per screenshot, is both
complete and legible, and is the setting to use here.
189 pages, 0 broken links.

commits.subject: Roadmap route 7: say that the index itself was put on trial, and passed
commits.body:
Every Rosario null here rests on a 1945 typescript. The register was read act by
act across 750 consecutive baptisms and agrees with it everywhere. He is not
there, and the index is not the reason.

commits.subject: Read the register itself, act by act, to the end of the volume - 750 baptisms
commits.body:
Every Rosario null in this archive rests on a TYPESCRIPT INDEX compiled in 1945
from the parish registers. Whether that typescript is complete had never been
tested - and an index is exactly the kind of evidence this archive has been
burned by before. This is the test.
The act-by-act read stopped in April. It has been carried to the end of the
volume: images 243 to 309. Three of those frames are duplicate exposures (257,
264, 300), and at two openings the filmer laid a loose certificate on the book,
covering one page - each read from the facing frame (284/285, 301/302). The
volume ends at act 862, on 22 July 1882.
METHOD, REFINED. Every act carries the child's name in the LEFT MARGIN in large
script. So rather than render a whole opening, the two margin strips - tile
columns 0-3 and 10-14 at level 13 - are rendered SIDE BY SIDE in one image. One
screenshot per opening, eight names legible at a glance. It is about four times
faster than reading the opening, and more accurate, because the names are at
full resolution rather than at 42%.
  Acts 113 to 862. 1 February to 22 July 1882. Seven hundred and fifty
  baptisms. No Lerena, in any spelling.
That is the first two-thirds of the year in which Pablo Armando Lerena was born
on 22 February, read from the register rather than from the index.
TWO NEAR MISSES, LOGGED AND RESOLVED RATHER THAN PASSED OVER:
  Armando Juan Rouillon, act 546, born 26 April 1882 - an ARMANDO baptised at
  Rosario in 1882, but born two months after Pablo Armando, and a Rouillon.
  Pablo Jacinto Gauna, act 827, 11 July 1882 - a PABLO whose margin surname was
  ambiguous at reading size. It was re-rendered at full magnification
  specifically in case it read LARENA, which is an attested variant of this
  family's name. It reads Gauna.
AND THE RESULT THAT MATTERS. Across 750 consecutive acts, everywhere the index
says there is no Lerena, the register says the same. THE INDEX AND THE REGISTER
AGREE. He is not there - and the index is not the reason he is not there.
That is a negative, but a load-bearing one. It means the Rosario nulls can be
trusted, and the search belongs somewhere else.
189 pages, 0 broken links.

commits.subject: Run the dispensation errand the same night, and close one branch of the question
commits.body:
The last errand written today was the Arquidiocesis de Montevideo marriage-
dispensation register, 1856-1932, as the shortest way at Juan Carlos Lerena. It
is done.
The reasoning was narrow and worth restating. Pablo Armando's enrolment card
names his mother MARIA LERENA, written with her husband's surname, and this
archive has never been able to tell whether that is her maiden name or her
married one. If it is her maiden name, she and Juan Carlos were kin - and a
marriage between kin needs a dispensation.
The register is in the full-text corpus, so it can be searched by its own
formulae: "Lerena el impedimento" catches a Lerena groom, "Lerena feligresa"
catches a Lerena bride, who is always named with her parish.
EIGHT Lerena dispensations in seventy-six years, in two families - the Montevideo
patricians of the Catedral (Mercedes 1883, Clorinda, Zelmira Carlota) and the
rural Lerenas of Trinidad in Flores (Juan Gualberto, Antonina and Maria in June
1885, Juan in 1894, Florinda Juana in 1909).
  There is no Juan Carlos Lerena in the register.
  There is no Lerena-Lerena dispensation in it at all.
Every Lerena in it marries OUT: Fernandez, Pelaez, Alvarez, Cordero, Marquez,
Autrias.
WHAT THAT NARROWS. If Maria was a Lerena by birth AND they married in the
archdiocese of Montevideo, a dispensation would exist. It does not. So either
she was not a Lerena by birth - the card giving her married name, which some
clerks did - or the marriage happened somewhere other than Montevideo.
WHAT IT PLAINLY DOES NOT DO is show they did not marry in Montevideo. This
register catches only two things: kin dispensations, and dispensations of the
three conciliar proclamas. A marriage between unrelated people with all three
proclamas duly read needed no dispensation and leaves no trace here whatsoever.
A negative from a register that records only exceptions is a weak negative, and
it is filed as one on the open-questions page and in the data.

FamilySearch firewalled this session". It has now been worked, so it says what

MARRIAGE DISPENSATION register, 1856-1932. If Maria was a Lerena by birth, the

full-text corpus; it surfaced in today's searching.
Also a new section on the sources page recording which places FamilySearch full

Santa Fe is NOT in the corpus, which is why Rosario took eighty openings;

commits.subject: Follow the girl from folio 229 to her wedding, and defuse a name coincidence
commits.body:
FamilySearch's full-text search reads handwriting across un-indexed images. It
does NOT cover Santa Fe - which is why Rosario had to be read by eye, eighty
openings of it. It DOES cover Montevideo. Given the phrase "Maria Lerena" it
returned a marriage register, and the image was opened rather than trusted.
  San Francisco de Asis, Ciudad Vieja, Montevideo. Folio 364, act 1879.
  Los tres de Noviembre de mil ochocientos ochenta y seis ... el matrimonio que
  por palabras de presente contrajo Don Jaime Herrera, soltero, hijo legitimo
  del Doctor Don Nicolas y de Dona Adela Crucet, con Dona Maria Lerena, soltera,
  hija legitima de Don Luis Lerena y de Dona Julia Juanico.
She is the child of folio 229. Born at Rosario on 8 October 1865, baptised there
on 17 February 1866 to Luis Lerena Lenguas and Julia Juanico - and twenty-one
years old, in Montevideo, on 3 November 1886. The parents match by name in a
second, independent, PRIMARY act, in another country, twenty years later.
That matters beyond the pleasure of it. It lifts the Rosario couple from "one
act plus user-submitted genealogy" to TWO PRIMARY ACTS. Luis Lerena and Julia
Juanico were a real Montevideo couple; their daughter was born on the Argentine
bank and married on the Uruguayan one. The only Lerena in a hundred and seventy
years of the Rosario parish register went home.
A detail worth keeping: the witnesses are the groom's father and the BRIDE'S
MOTHER. Luis Lerena is not at his own daughter's wedding. He may have been dead
by 1886 - the act does not say so, and that is marked as inference.
AND THE TRAP, SAID OUT LOUD. Pablo Armando Lerena's mother is named on his 1908
enrolment card as MARIA LERENA. This is a DIFFERENT Maria Lerena. She married
Jaime Herrera in November 1886, four years after Pablo Armando was born, and she
was sixteen years old in February 1882. She cannot be his mother. A rare
surname, a common forename and a strong wish for the pieces to fit is exactly
how this archive has gone wrong before - so it is written down on the page,
before anyone is caught by it.
Two more negatives from the same corpus: full-text for "Juan Carlos Lerena"
returns exactly two hits in the whole of it - a 1922 Montevideo marriage
dispensation for Juan Carlos Gonzalez Lerena, and a 2001 death - neither ours.
Full-text for "Armando Lerena" returns two, both Colombian.

commits.subject: Sancho de Llerena - hypothesis 1's own test, met, and answering the other way
commits.body:
Following the 1866 Rosario act back through the FamilySearch Tree produced the
Montevideo trunk, and at its root a soldier:
  Sancho Llerena Aguilar, b. Cordoba, Andalusia, 1767; m. Maria Josefa Fernandez
  Tresguerras at Canelones, Uruguay, 8 January 1791; resident Montevideo; d. 1832.
He is the great-grandfather of BOTH the Lerena Lenguas and the Lerena Traibel -
so of Luis Lerena Lenguas, the father named in the Rosario act, and of Gilberto
Justiniano Lerena Lenguas of the Argentine Stud Book. The two branches even
marry back together: Carlos Ambrosio Lerena Traibel married his cousin Luisa
Lerena Lenguas at San Francisco, Montevideo, in 1867.
Fourteen Uruguayan parish records are attached to Sancho. They spell him LERENA
in 1793, 1840 and 1858; LLERENA in 1804, 1811, 1827 and 1830; and once, in 1828,
SANCHO DE LLERENA.
Since 8 September, hypothesis 1 has named exactly this as the thing that would
settle it - "whether Lerena and Llerena ever alternate for one person in early
River Plate records". They do. And "de Llerena" is the toponymic construction,
of Llerena, the Badajoz town; a Basque house-name in -ena does not take de.
The distribution argument is not overturned, and both pages say so. La Rioja
really is the one dense Spanish cluster of the spelling Lerena, at forty times
the national average. What has changed is that it need not be THIS something.
Both can be true: a Basque-formed Lerena of the upper Ebro, and separately a
River Plate Lerena that is a reduction of Andalusian Llerena, carried over by
one man in the 1780s and smoothed to a single l by Uruguayan clerks inside a
generation. Only the second bears on this family - and the only Lerena trunk yet
found in the River Plate is a Llerena.
TIER: the trunk is FamilySearch Tree, user-submitted and editable by anyone, and
the decision that those fourteen records are one man is a tree user's, not this
archive's. The acts have not been opened. What anyone can check is the narrower
fact: the Uruguayan registers spell this family both ways. And nothing connects
the trunk to Pablo Armando - no Juan Carlos appears anywhere in it.
ALSO IN THIS COMMIT, A CORRECTION TO MY OWN WORK FROM AN HOUR AGO. The table
published this evening said the Arturo Lerena of drawer Cajon 985 was born at
Montevideo in 1858, son of Avelino Lerena and Ambrosia Traibel. That conflated
two men. The Uruguayan record it rested on gives the spouse as EMA REGULES - and
Ema Regules married JUAN ARTURO Lerena Traibel (1861-1936), children born at
Montevideo 1881-87. The drawer's Arturo married AMALIA DIAZ, children born in La
Pampa, Mendoza and Entre Rios 1889-97. Two men, one surname, one given name. The
row is withdrawn, "four branches" is now three, and it is on the corrections
page. It was caught by going to the underlying record, which is the same move
this archive keeps having to relearn.

commits.subject: A base rate from evidence already on the shelf, and one new Armando Lerena
commits.body:
FamilySearch let this session back in, so the Uruguayan lead was worked
properly.
FIRST, THE NEGATIVE, because it is worth as much. There is no Juan Carlos
Lerena born in Uruguay between 1830 and 1870 in Uruguay Catholic Church Records
1726-2000, in Uruguay Civil Registration 1879-2020, or in the Uruguay Baptisms
1750-1900 index; and no Lerena groom marrying a Maria in Uruguay between 1865
and 1885. Every Juan Carlos Lerena the index returns is a twentieth-century
civil-registration card, decades too late. The indexed record does not hand him
over. What that narrows is which UN-indexed pages are worth turning.
SECOND, A BASE RATE, built entirely from data this archive already had. Pablo
Armando's enrolment card sits in army drawer "Cajon 985 (Lera)", filed by SOUND
rather than spelling, so its Lerena section is a near-complete roll of Argentine
Lerena men of enrolment age - each card naming his father and mother. It was
read on 10 September to confirm no card but his names a Juan Carlos and a Maria.
It still doesn't. But the FATHERS were never followed up. Four of them trace:
  Gilberto Lerena x Julia Salvanach     - Montevideo, 24 May 1855
  Alejandro M. Lerena x Julia Bassani   - Uruguay, 1839; a son born Montevideo 1886
  Arturo Lerena x Amalia Diaz           - Montevideo, 1858; son of Avelino Lerena
                                          and Ambrosia Traibel
  Nemesio Ramon Lerena x Laura Escobite - married at Salto, Uruguay, 1903, then
                                          Concordia, Entre Rios, across the river
Four branches, four different provinces of settlement, one common origin. Three
more could not be traced either way.
It is NOT a link - none of these men is Juan Carlos Lerena, and none is shown to
be related to him. It is a base rate: in this generation an Argentine Lerena is a
Uruguayan family's son far more often than not, in every traceable case in the
one drawer where they are gathered together. Juan Carlos Lerena, who left no
trace whatever in the province where his son was born, fits that shape.
THIRD, ONE NEW NAME, recorded and not claimed. Armando Lerena, aged 26, married,
entry 28 on a Buenos Aires - Montevideo crossing of January or February 1910.
The clerk wrote his nationality in the manifest in his own hand: ORIENTAL. Read
from the image at tile level 13, not from the index - the house rule.
He is NOT Pablo Armando. Wrong nationality: Pablo Armando enrolled with the
Argentine army in 1908 and carried an Argentine passport in 1940. The age is two
years out. And in 1910 Pablo Armando was at the Cape and unmarried - he and Mary
Septima did not marry until September 1911, six years after their first son was
born. But an Armando Lerena, Uruguayan, of almost exactly his age is the shape a
brother or a first cousin would have, and Armando is not a common given name on
these lists. He goes on the register as unplaced, which is what the evidence
supports and no more.

commits.subject: Bring the front page up to date with the sweep and the Uruguayan turn
commits.body:
Three changes on the home page, all of them things that stopped being true
today.
The headline figure "1879-1901 - every year of the Rosario baptism index" is now
"1731-1901 - both volumes, read end to end, and the surname appears exactly
once". A new figure sits beside it: "Uruguayan - what the act behind that one
Lerena says of her parents".
The paragraph about the missing baptism said the sweep covered 1879-1901 and
called the result "a sharp question rather than a blank wall". It is now sharper
than that. Across both volumes and a hundred and seventy years the surname
appears once - so it is not only his baptism that is missing, but his brothers
and sisters, and his father's marriage, and every trace of the household. A
family that lives in a parish leaves baptisms. This one leaves nothing.
And a new paragraph for the one Lerena who is there: folio 229, February 1866,
Don Luis Lerena Lenguas and Dona Julia Juanico, "naturales del E. Oriental" -
with the godfather standing by proxy from the other side of the river. Published
Uruguayan genealogy makes them the Lerena Lenguas of Montevideo, one of whose
sons co-founded the Argentine Stud Book. Nothing links the two houses yet, and
the page says so.
Also 125 people in the register becomes 129.

commits.subject: Rewrite the roadmap, which still thought his parents were unknown
commits.body:
The roadmap was the most out-of-date page in the archive. It opened with "Who
were Pablo Armando Lerena's parents? ... above him there is nothing at all", and
route 1 was headed "needs an email" - all of which stopped being true on 10
September, when the 1908 army enrolment card was finally opened and named Juan
Carlos Lerena and Maria Lerena. Three days of findings had gone in around it
without anyone going back to the page that tells a reader what to do next.
Rewritten around the state as it actually is:
- The question that started it, and its answer, including the fact that the
  answering document was written off for a month on objections that turned out
  to be machine-index artefacts.
- The question that replaced it: who were Juan Carlos and Maria, and where did
  they come from - with the three full-index negatives set out as three panels,
  because together they say something a single negative does not. A household
  that lives in a parish leaves baptisms; this one leaves nothing.
- The answer that now leads: they were not a Rosario family, and the one Lerena
  in that parish in a hundred and seventy years was Uruguayan.
- Seven routes reranked. Montevideo is now route 1. Rosario is route 7 and
  marked closed - do not reopen without a new reason. The two letters that are
  out are marked as out and waited on rather than as things to do.
Also updated open question 1 with the sharper version of the missing baptism,
and added the one thing a stranger could most usefully tell this archive: does
anyone hold a Uruguayan Lerena line with a Juan Carlos born in the 1840s or
1850s, married to a Maria.
