commits.subject: The horses page had guessed it five days early
commits.body:
On 8 September the horses page said, of Gilberto Justiniano Lerena Lenguas:
  "Lerena Lenguas is a River Plate double surname and Lenguas is Uruguayan -
   consistent with the name's Uruguayan density and with Stud Oriental,
   oriental being the ordinary Argentine word for Uruguayan."
That was an inference from two words on a Wikipedia page. Five days later the
Rosario baptism act said it outright: Don Luis Lerena Lenguas and Dona Julia
Juanico, naturales del E. Oriental. And published Uruguayan genealogy makes that
Luis a brother of Gilberto, both sons of Luis Lerena y Fernandez (1811-1878) and
Justiniana Lenguas Gonzalez of Montevideo - with the child at folio 229 carrying
Justiniana as her fifth given name, for that grandmother.
So the block is added where the guess was made, rather than quietly editing the
guess into a fact. It still claims no relationship to Pablo Armando, and it still
marks the Montevideo generations SECONDARY.

commits.subject: Narrow the LERINA exclusions - they were right, for partly the wrong reason
commits.body:
This archive's own search box flagged it: all four LERINA entries carried the
same label, EXCLUDED, with the same unexamined sentence behind it -
  "LERINA here is an Italian surname, not a variant of the Spanish Lerena."
That is a claim about the NAME, not about the people, reached from an index
without opening a manifest. It is the identical move that got the Armando Lorena
card wrong and had to be corrected in public a fortnight ago.
The exclusion itself survives, and on much firmer ground. The four arrive at
Buenos Aires on 15 March 1889 aged 59, 55, 21 and 17 - seven years after Pablo
Armando was born at Rosario - and the party contains no Juan Carlos and no Maria.
None of them can be anyone sought. That rests on facts in the index, not on a
judgement about surnames. The surname claim is withdrawn as a reason and the
withdrawal is on the corrections page.
Also updated hypothesis 1b, the Italian hypothesis, which took a second blow
today. The Rosario baptism index has now been read end to end and the one Lerena
in it is a Uruguayan of the Montevideo patriciate - a Lerena Lenguas married to a
Juanico with an Oribe in the generation above. The surname has a documented home
in the River Plate and it is not Liguria.
What still stands for the Italian reading, and is not dismissed: the death
certificate says LERINA, and nothing found today explains that.

commits.subject: Follow the act to Montevideo - and meet the Stud Book Lerenas coming the other way
commits.body:
The 1866 act named the father Luis Lerena Lenguas and the godfather, standing by
proxy, Don Luis Lerena. That pair of names is enough to find the household in
published Uruguayan genealogy.
Luis Lerena y Fernandez (1811-1878), widower of Carolina Oribe Ladron de Guevara,
married secondly Justiniana Lenguas Gonzalez, daughter of Gen. Pedro Lenguas
Grandal. Their children carry the compound Lerena Lenguas. This is the Montevideo
patriciate - Oribe is the family of the President.
Two things follow. The proxy godfather gets a name: the child's paternal
grandfather, in Montevideo. And the child's fifth given name is JUSTINIANA, for
that grandmother - so the act and the genealogy are describing one family, and
neither was written with the other in view.
And one of those sons is already in this archive. Gilberto Justiniano Lerena
Lenguas, Montevideo 1855-1912, co-founder of the ARGENTINE STUD BOOK, breeder of
the Quadruple Crown winner Old Man, the man for whom a Group 1 at Palermo was
renamed in 1914. He has sat in this register since the 1895 Buenos Aires census
marked UNPLACED - HIGH INTEREST, for a reason that had nothing to do with
Uruguay: Pablo Armando Lerena trained and owned racehorses.
That was always the loudest coincidence in the file and it was set aside as a
coincidence. It still is one. But the parish register of Rosario and the turf of
Buenos Aires now arrive at the same Montevideo house from opposite ends, by
methods that share no assumption.
A third, smaller convergence, noticed looking back: a findmypast index row copied
down on 9 September - "Emma Liseta, 1876, father Luis, mother Julia, Uruguay" -
is the same couple, a younger sister of the child at folio 229. The evidence was
already on the shelf; it had no shape to sit in.
EVIDENCE TIERS, because this is exactly where an archive goes wrong. The act is
primary and was read at full resolution; everything in it stands. Everything
about the Montevideo generations above it is SECONDARY - Geneanet, Geni, a
genealogical blog - and none cites a source checkable from here. They agree with
each other and with a document they were not written from. That is the best that
can be said until the Montevideo registers are opened, and it is not proof.
data/montevideo-lerena-lenguas.tsv marks every row PRIMARY or SECONDARY.
And none of it links Juan Carlos Lerena to this family. What has changed is where
to look next.
Also in this commit: FamilySearch firewalled the search endpoints partway through
(Incapsula, after the day's reading), so the Montevideo work was done from other
sources and the register browse left alone.

commits.subject: Open the act at folio 229 - and the family turns out to be Uruguayan
commits.body:
The index entry found this morning had an act behind it. Rosario, Bautismos
1865-1867, image 124 of 311, folio 229, act 1541, ark 3:1:S3HT-XS9C-ZL.
Handwritten; read at full tile resolution in four overlapping renders.
  Es hija legitima de Don Luis Lerena Lenguas y de Dona Julia Juanico,
  naturales del E. Oriental; fueron padrinos Don Luis Lerena, representado
  por don Claudino Campos y Dona Margarita Mara de Carlos.
Born 8 October 1865, baptised 17 February 1866. And the parents are stated in
the act itself to be naturales del Estado Oriental - natives of Uruguay.
So the only Lerena baptised at Rosario between 1731 and 1901 is a Uruguayan.
The mother is a Juanico and the father a Lerena Lenguas, both Montevideo names
rather than Santa Fe ones. And the godfather - another Don Luis Lerena, probably
the child's grandfather - did not attend: he was represented by proxy, which is
what people do when the godfather is across the river.
That makes sense of four negatives at once. No Rosario baptism for Pablo
Armando; none for Juan Carlos; no Lerena marriage at Rosario 1867-1885; no
Lerena in the parish index at all but this one. A family that lives in a parish
leaves baptisms. This one leaves nothing, because it was somewhere else.
Stated carefully, because it would be easy to overstate: NO LINK HAS BEEN SHOWN
between Luis Lerena Lenguas and Juan Carlos Lerena. Two men sharing a surname in
one city sixteen years apart is a lead. The 1866 child is not Pablo Armando's
sister. And Pablo Armando himself was born at Rosario, documented twice over.
Where the DNA sits, honestly: the Rio de la Plata genetic group spans both
banks. It cannot tell Buenos Aires from Montevideo and never could. What it says
is that the Argentine and Uruguayan hypotheses are genetically the same
hypothesis.
Added: notes/the-uruguayan-turn.md; data/rosario-1866-act-1541.tsv with the full
transcription; hypothesis 1c; four people in the register (the child, both
parents, the proxy godfather), all marked UNPLACED; two errands pointing at
Uruguay, Registros Parroquiales 1750-1930; and a "Closed" group on the errands
page, since one errand was opened and finished in the same afternoon.

commits.subject: Read the pre-1879 index end to end, and find the only Lerena in it
commits.body:
Film 004530324, the Rosario baptism index for 1731-1879, letters L-Q. The L
section runs from image 6 to image 85; image 86 begins the M section. Every
opening between has now been opened and read at tile level 12, whole opening to
a screen, anything ambiguous re-rendered at level 13.
Eighty openings. Eight of them (35-42) are the roll break - target card, blanks,
"continua en el proximo rollo", "ARGN-0030 rollo 28", "rollo 29",
"continuacion". Nothing is lost across the join; image 43 re-shoots image 34.
Images 63 and 83 are duplicate exposures. That leaves seventy openings of actual
index, continuous from 1731 to 1879.
One name:
  LERENA LENGUAS, Maria Julia Margarita Josefa E.J. - 1866, Libro 15, folio 229
Image 58, ark 9Q97-Y3S2-FPP. The 1945 typist cross-indexed her a line above
under LENGUAS, same year, same folio - which is how we know the compound is real
and not a slip: a Lerena father and a Lenguas mother. Confirmed at full
resolution before it was believed, which is the lesson of the Armando Lorena
card taken to heart.
She is not Pablo Armando's sister - sixteen years too early, compound where he
is simple. What she establishes is harder and more useful. Both volumes of the
Rosario baptism index have now been read end to end, and across a hundred and
seventy years the surname occurs once. Pablo Armando's own baptism is not in it.
The family leaves no trace in the parish before him or after him. Whatever
brought Juan Carlos Lerena and Maria to Rosario, they were not a Rosario family.
The act at folio 229 names both parents and has not been read. It is now the
first errand on the list.
Five near-misses re-rendered and recorded so nobody checks them twice: Lerones
(1856), "Lesa (o Lera)" (1857), Loveras (1864), Lerre Echeita (1870), Lensina
(1816, read at first glance as Leprina).
Also honest: reading eighty openings in an afternoon got this archive
rate-limited by FamilySearch for the second time in four days. Both blocks were
mine, not theirs.

commits.subject: Open the pre-1879 baptism index - ten openings, and say what is unread
commits.body:
The best untried item on the list, and the first film this archive has opened
that could hold the generation ABOVE Pablo Armando.
Film 004530324, 554 images. Title card at image 5: "Parroquia N. S. del Rosario
- INDICE DE BAUTISMOS - VOLUMEN 3o - Anos 1731-1879 - LETRAS L-Q - Revisado y
Restaurado en 1945". The companion to the 1879-1900 volume: same restoration,
same typescript, same four columns.
Everything read until now began in 1879 - three years after his birth, fine for
him and useless for everyone above him. This is where Juan Carlos Lerena's own
baptism would sit if he was born in the city, and where an older brother or
sister of Pablo Armando would sit if the family were there in the 1870s.
TEN OPENINGS READ IN FULL, spread to bound the section: 1731, 1740-55, 1826-29,
1843-44, 1852-58. No Lerena in any of them. The names that recur for a century
and a half are Leguizamon, Lencina, Lopez, Ledesma, Lescano, Ludueña, Lucero,
Leiva, Luna, Leon, Lujan, Llanos. Two near misses recorded: LERONES (1856) and
"LESA (o LERA)" (1857), where the index itself offers Lera as an alternative
reading of the same hand. Image 43 is a duplicate - the second roll re-shoots
the first roll's last page.
AND THE IMPORTANT HALF: images 8-19, 21-27, 29-33 and everything from 49 onward
are UNREAD - and 49 onward is 1858 to 1879, the whole window for an older
sibling and much of the window for Juan Carlos. The part that matters most is
the part still unread. Recorded so nobody mistakes ten openings for a sweep.
Resume at image 49, ark 9Q97-Y3S2-FLK.
METHOD NOTE KEPT: the tile-retry loop must re-request the SAME url. A
cache-busting query returns a different tile and silently scrambles the mosaic -
it produced one unreadable, misaligned page before it was caught.

- notes/the-index-before-1879.md, findings.md
- /searched/ leads with it, gaps and all

commits.subject: Find the only grave, at Maitland Woltemade
commits.body:
FamilySearch had signed the session out, so the afternoon went to untried
non-FamilySearch sources. The third produced the first physical trace of this
family found anywhere.
A GRAVE KERB at Maitland, Woltemade Cemetery, Cape Town - poured concrete
edging, not a headstone - with one word cut into its face:
  LERENA
No forename, no dates, no epitaph. Above it, bare earth and grass. Photographed
by Heather MacAlister, published through the eGGSA Gravestone Photograph
Library, album "Le", image 85 of 127, page dated 5 May 2021. Eighty-seven people
had looked at it before this archive did.
MAITLAND WOLTEMADE IS WHERE BOTH OF THEM ARE BURIED - Mary Septima, grave
7719A, November 1935; Pablo Armando, "Maitland Cemetery no 1", March 1950. And
it is the only Lerena grave in the whole Western Cape collection. Variants
checked the same afternoon: LERIN, which would catch Lerina and Lerini, returns
nothing; "Lerena" as a substring also covers Llerena, with no separate hit;
LAREN returns 39 records, every one Clarence or its like.
IT CANNOT BE ASSIGNED TO A PERSON, and is not. A surname on a kerb with no dates
is equally consistent with her grave, his, or a family plot holding both. The
grave number would settle it, and the municipal cemetery office holds the
Woltemade register.
ONE SMALL THING IT DOES SAY: the stone reads LERENA - which runs, lightly,
against the hypothesis raised from the DNA that the name might be nearer LERINA,
the spelling on his death certificate. Not decisive; a kerb may postdate a
burial and a mason cuts what he is given. But it is evidence and it points the
other way.
THE PHOTOGRAPH IS NOT REPRODUCED ON THE SITE. eGGSA's terms allow fair personal
use with credit and forbid replication into another website database, so this
archive records the facts - which are not copyrightable - links to the image,
and names the photographer.
- notes/the-only-grave.md, data/the-grave.tsv
- /south-africa/ gains "The only grave"
- NEW /photograph-these/ - 6 Cape Town places, the kerb first, each saying what
  the picture would settle and what to capture, because the kerb alone is not
  enough: the whole plot is wanted, with section and row markers
- 181 pages, 0 broken links
Also checked: no replies yet from the Army, the Cancilleria or the Western Cape
Archives. Three days is nothing for an archive.

commits.subject: Amsterdam answers: no Lerena in the Latin American left press
commits.body:
The IISH replied to the 9 September letter. Their Latin American periodicals,
Argentinian included, are digitised and OCR'd as "Latin American Anarchist and
Labour Periodicals Online, c. 1880-1940" at degruyterbrill.com/database/lalp.
Their archivist searched Lerena and its variants: nothing popped up. They will
scan specific items at 0.50 euro each but cannot research on our behalf.
RE-RUN HERE the same day, because "nothing" is a weaker record than a
description of the noise:
  Lerena - 171 hits, almost all the CONDE DE LERENA (Charles III's finance
  minister, whose 1787 Censo is quoted in Spanish economic history) and
  "Osimani y Llerena", a STREET in Montevideo where the anarchist weekly La
  Tierra had its office.
  Lerina - 16 hits, every one OCR breakage of "ballerina".
No person of this family in the Latin American left press, 1880-1940.
AND THE WEIGHT OF THAT, STATED RATHER THAN BANKED. It is the WEAKEST of the
three objections to the family tradition. A horse-dealer in his twenties would
not be in the anarchist press unless he were notable, and most people never
appear in any periodical at all. Absence from a newspaper corpus is close to no
evidence about an ordinary man.
The objection that actually bites is the enrolment card: in 1908 he walked into
his own government's consular office at Cape Town and wrote down his name, his
class, his birthplace and both his parents. A man hiding from the Argentine
state does not do that. And Ley 4144 deported foreigners, not nationals - the
mechanism the story implies could not have been used on him.
Not disproved. Now unlikely. The AGN expulsion files remain the only place that
could settle it positively, and that one still needs David.

commits.subject: Compare against the Defranceski archive, and correct myself twice
commits.body:
David asked for a side-by-side against TheDefranceski and the Defranceski
project. It forced two corrections before producing anything useful.
THE PALETTE. I said earlier the Lerena tokens matched Falco's, then that they
were a deliberate cool variant. Both wrong. The Lerena styles.css root block is
BYTE-IDENTICAL to Defranceski's - every token, same typefaces, same --maxw.
Lerena inherited the Defranceski system exactly; FALCO is the outlier with a
warm palette.
THE SCALE. Defranceski: 65 pages, 38 components. Lerena: 21 and 2. Mostly depth,
not defect - so the list is dominated by what is absent rather than wrong.
THREE THINGS THAT ARE WRONG, because this site contradicts itself:
1. The living-person rule is broken by our own pages. The footer says living
   people are excluded; /direct-line/ publishes a living person's name, exact
   birth date, two cities and both marriages, under a chip reading "Omitted" and
   a caption reading "Details withheld". Defranceski's rule is different and
   workable: by name only, no dates, no places, no photographs. Pick one and
   honour it. The present state claims a protection it does not provide - and
   /dna/ now sits on top of it.
2. Two chip vocabularies on one site: the home page advertises Documented /
   Inferred / Family lore while the register uses Connected / Excluded /
   Unplaced.
3. The footer promises corrections with nowhere to put them. This archive has
   made at least eight documented corrections in a fortnight and they are buried
   in notes.
And the mechanical reason our register links 5 rows out of 125: Defranceski
stores a bare FamilySearch id and builds the URL with an ark() helper. We store
whole URLs, so we mostly store nothing.
Full list - fix, add, improve, remove - in
notes/compared-with-the-defranceski-archive.md. Nothing has been changed on the
site yet; this commit is the audit.

commits.subject: Record the other five genetic groups - they argue against my own hypothesis
commits.body:
The slider went to low confidence: 8 of 8 groups. Five legible - South Africa;
South Africa and Zimbabwe; Argentina (Corrientes and Buenos Aires), Uruguay and
Paraguay; England; Ireland (Cork, Kerry and Limerick) and England. Three sit
below the fold, unseen.
NO ITALIAN GROUP among the five. That is evidence against hypothesis 1b, which
was written an hour earlier, and it is recorded as such rather than left out. It
does not kill the hypothesis - a cluster needs enough tested people with
documented trees, and an Italian great-grandparent's group can fail to form -
but the easiest confirmation was available and did not appear.
The asymmetry stated plainly on the page: the Rio de la Plata group is a
POSITIVE result, a cluster formed at high confidence from 178 kits. The Italian
claim rests on a NEGATIVE - no Iberian - plus arithmetic on 11.1%. Not the same
class of evidence.
And the eight groups strengthen what was already proved. Every group except the
Rio de la Plata one is accounted for by her other three grandparents: two South
African, two British Isles. A clean four-grandparent reading, which makes the
Argentine group harder to explain away, not easier.
Technical note recorded: the confidence slider governs the genetic groups only.
The ethnicity percentages are identical in both views.

commits.subject: Add the DNA - a third leg under Argentina, and an Italian hypothesis
commits.body:
A granddaughter of Pablo Armando has tested at MyHeritage. She is LIVING, so
this archive omits her: not named, ethnicity profile not published, and only
the figures that bear on Pablo Armando - dead since 1950 - are recorded.
WHAT IT SETTLES. A high-confidence genetic group, "Argentina (Corrientes and
Buenos Aires), Uruguay and Paraguay", built from 178 kits, 61 with trees. That
is people sharing actual chromosome segments whose documented trees converge on
the Rio de la Plata, and it can only have come from him - her other three
grandparents are English Devon and Cape Afrikaner.
The Argentine origin now stands on three independent legs: the 1940 passport,
the 1908 enrolment card, and a chromosome. A fortnight ago it stood on one. And
the group's top places for 1900-1950 name SANTA FE - the first time anything
outside the family's own paperwork has pointed at that province.
WHAT IT QUESTIONS. Iberian 0.0%. Italian 11.1% (North 6.1, South 3.6, Sardinian
1.4). There is no Spanish component at all, where a Spanish-descended criollo
great-grandfather should show as roughly 25% in a granddaughter. The Italian has
no other source in her tree, and at one quarter implies about 44% in him - one
Italian parent - northern-dominant.
WHY IT WOULD EXPLAIN A LOT. A couple who married in Italy before emigrating
would never appear in the Rosario marriage register, now read clean 1867-1885.
The register around his birth is full of Ligurian and Piedmontese names. And his
death was registered LERINA, treated here for a month as a clerk's slip - while
CEMLA records Lerina as an ITALIAN surname arriving from Genova. The "error" may
be the one document that got it right.
Stated as a hypothesis, not a finding. Ethnicity estimates are not records, the
noise at one quarter is large, and MyHeritage distributes Iberian awkwardly. The
genetic group is the stronger signal and it says Rio de la Plata, not Italian.
CONSEQUENCE FOR THE WORK: the Rosario sweeps recorded no Lerena, Llerena, Larena
or Lorena - LERINA was never separately looked for, and it sorts adjacent.

commits.subject: Read the 1882 register act by act, and test the index
commits.body:
The block lifted after an hour. Three more things done.
THE REGISTER ITSELF. Every Rosario null this archive holds rests on a TYPESCRIPT
index, and whether the typist missed anything had never been tested. Libro 24
was read act by act - film 004098792, waypoint "Bautismos 1881-1882". Every act
carries the child's name in the margin; all 183 margins in the span were read.
  1 February to 15 March 1882 - acts 113 to 295, pages 390 to 435 - no Lerena.
He was born 22 February. Three weeks either side of his birth, nothing skipped.
The book also gave up a rate: 112 baptisms in January 1882, 122 in February -
four a day. The first denominator this archive has had.
A filming detail worth keeping: page 425 carries a slip pasted on 29 May 1905
that hides four acts, and the NEXT FRAME is the same page refilmed with the slip
lifted. Nothing is lost. Also one plain duplicate exposure at image 225.
What it settles: the index is not hiding him, at least not here - register and
index agree, so "perhaps the typist missed it" is no longer available.
What it does NOT: six weeks is not a year. April, 1883, or an adult baptism are
all still open. The stopping point is recorded so the sweep can be resumed
exactly - about 130 more frames to finish 1882.
THE LDS HOUSEHOLD CARD exists as an image but is FamilySearch-Centre-only, the
same wall as the Cape estate file. Ricardo is "Relationship to Head of
Household: Son", so the card lists a household with a head - almost certainly
Pablo Armando, in the month Mary Septima died.
THE CONSULATE THAT SHOULD NOT EXIST. Argentina and South Africa established
diplomatic relations only on 10 September 1947, and the earliest consulate the
histories mention is 1938. Yet this family holds Argentine documents proving a
consular office at Cape Town in 1908 and 1940 - thirty-nine years early. Not a
contradiction: consular relations are not diplomatic relations, and the usual
instrument is the honorary consul. A. B. Bayne is not a Spanish name. So the
"Consul General" tradition is not proved but is now EXPLICABLE, which is a
different and more honest thing. And a man fleeing Argentina as a communist does
not put his name, class, birthplace and parents on his own government's form in
1908 - evidence against the other tradition, recorded as such.

9, 1884, folio 20 now reads LAVENA V. x BELMONTE A. beyond argument.
PARTLY DONE - Gilberto Justiniano Lerena Lenguas, b. 24 May 1855, d. 8 Dec 1912,
m. Julia Salvanach. Founded Stud Oriental 1887; promoter, founder and Secretary
of the Stud Book Argentino, signing its first act 11 June 1893; bred Old Man;
Haras El Viejo and five other studs; the Premio Abril renamed for him in 1914.
The Lerena Lenguas were Uruguayan and rich - Luis Lerena Lenguas had a
fifteen-room house at Juanico photographed for the 1889 Paris exhibition.
Nothing connects him to Pablo Armando, and the temptation to imply otherwise is
refused in the note rather than in a footnote. The two sources that would answer
the only useful question - was there a Juan Carlos in that family - are behind
an hCaptcha (geni) and Cloudflare (Geneanet). Listed, not quietly dropped.
BLOCKED - items 1, 3 and 5. FamilySearch now returns "Access Denied - Error 15 -
blocked by our security service". After a day of heavy automated reading their

commits.subject: Read the L and Ll sections end to end, and close them
commits.body:
Done properly so it can be left behind, as David asked.
Every opening of the L section and of the Ll section, first to last, in order -
41 frames, 38 distinct and 3 duplicate exposures, each verified on arrival by
year and Libro/folio, running continuously from Libro 23 folio 145 to Libro 48
folio 546, covering 1879 to 1901.
  No Lerena. No Llerena. No Larena. No Lorena. In any year. In either section.
L opens at 1880 - there are no L entries for 1879 at all - and runs past 1900
into 1901. The whole Ll section across twenty-two years is twenty-six entries.
The nearest thing to the name is LLERA: Pedro (1898) and Ida C. (1900).
The Armandos: Lofre 1889, Lujan 1895, Lunardi 1895, Limonetti 1897. All after
1889, none in the right year. Armando looks like a name that came into fashion
at Rosario in the 1890s, which makes a boy christened Pablo Armando in February
1882 unusual for his date.
METHOD, which is the transferable part. The index is TYPEWRITTEN, not
handwritten - the obstacle was never the hand but the viewer's zoom.
FamilySearch serves the pages as DeepZoom tiles; level 13 for this film is
20 x 15 tiles of 257px, about 5100 x 3800 for an opening. Assembled into a plain
HTML grid at 42% scale, a whole opening fits one screen with every surname
legible. Image numbers drift between viewer states; the image ARK is stable and
is what the data file records.
What it does NOT settle is said plainly rather than glossed: he was not baptised
as an infant, or was baptised outside the cathedral's books, or the index itself
is incomplete - it is a later typescript compiled from the registers, not the
registers. That last is why an act-by-act reading of the 1882 register is still
worth doing one day.

commits.subject: Correct our own record: Chappell was a married name
commits.body:
Chasing the LDS Church Census entry found beside the enrolment card led to the
FamilySearch Family Tree, where a small branch for this family already exists.
Nobody has attached parents to Pablo Armando - the enrolment card is genuinely
new - but the branch carried something else.
This archive had Roque's first wife as "Rosalina Wilhelmina CHAPPELL" and
Ricardo's wife as "Doreen ?". Both wrong the same way:
  Roseline Wilhelmina FORBES m. Frederick Christian Chappell, 1 Nov 1920,
  Woodstock, Cape Town. Chappell died 1933. His widow married Roque Luis
  Armando Lerena in 1936. Her daughter Doreen May Chappell, b.1921, married
  Roque's brother Ricardo Juan Carlos Lerena.
Chappell was her MARRIED name; her maiden name was FORBES. The 1936 register
calls her "Rosaline Wilhermina Forbes Chappell" because that is what a
remarrying widow is called, and this archive read it as a maiden name.
Two brothers married a mother and her daughter.
Verified before writing: the 1920 marriage exists in BOTH the SA civil marriage
records and the Anglican parish registers, and Frederick Christian Chappell has
his own Western Cape estate file naming "Rose Forbes Chappell". What is NOT
proved is that this Doreen is that Doreen - that rests on the user-contributed
tree plus the surname, and is marked inferred on the page. A discrepancy over
her death year (1993 in the tree, estate advertised 2001) is left standing
rather than tidied away.
The naming discipline is now visible as a rule: this family gave the
grandparents' names back every generation, which is exactly why Ricardo Juan
Carlos b.1920 corroborates a card naming Juan Carlos Lerena.

commits.subject: Hunt Juan Carlos Lerena; run the full-text sweep at last
commits.body:
Four searches the day the name was found, four negatives, and one of them
closes an instrument the archive had been holding in reserve.
1. Lerena marriages in Argentina 1865-1885 - the window a man whose son was born
   in Feb 1882 would have married in. 2,531 results, no Juan Carlos. One new
   person recorded: Carolina Lerena, Buenos Aires.
2. Any Juan Lerena born 1840-1865. Not one Juan Carlos in Argentina or Uruguay.
   The Lerena Juans of that generation are Jalisco, Mexico (a large separate
   population, noted here for the first time), the Trinidad/Flores kindred, and
   one man in the Ecija census of 1903.
3. FULL-TEXT SEARCH, listed as the clearest remaining opening for two rounds,
   has now actually been swept. The surname is in the corpus in quantity -
   Arequipa, Valladolid, Madrid, Trinidad/Flores, Montevideo, Jalisco. Santa Fe
   is not in it. Rosario is not in it. Not thin - absent. The instrument does not
   cover the ground the question is on. Retired as a closed item rather than left
   open as a hope. A phrase search for "Juan Carlos Lerena" returns one man,
   Juan Carlos Gonzalez Lerena of Montevideo, b.1899; his 1922 marriage
   dispensation was read rather than assumed. Not ours.
4. The Cape estate images are still restricted, re-tested signed in.
Which leaves the death notice in MOOC 6/9/17017 - and it now carries a
prediction: question 19 should say Juan Carlos Lerena and Maria. If Maria's
entry has a maiden name, the one thing the card could not settle is settled in

commits.subject: Read the rest of Cajon 985, and publish the negative
commits.body:
Images 650-688 of the enrolment film swept through the viewer's Image Index
panel. Recorded in data/cajon-985-scan.tsv.
The drawer is filed by SOUND, not spelling: Lera, Lerena, Lorena, Serena, Sera,
Era, Leza, Perena, Perella and Hereijo are interfiled - by the army clerk in
1908, not by FamilySearch. Gilberto Lerena's family appears under five different
spellings on five cards. That is why the machine index reached "Lorena" and
"Serena" so easily.
Five Lerena families are in the drawer - Gilberto, Alejandro, Arturo, Ramon,
Carlos. All Entre Rios, Mendoza, Buenos Aires, Montevideo. None from Rosario de
Santa Fe; no father called Juan Carlos. No brother.
Published as a negative with its limits stated: enrolment abroad was voluntary
and consular, a brother who stayed in Argentina would be filed in his own
district, and a brother who never enrolled is nowhere at all.
- data/cajon-985-scan.tsv, notes/the-cape-town-enrolment-card.md
- /enrolment-card/ gains "The rest of the drawer"
- /searched/ leads with the search that worked, and why it had already been
  thrown away once

commits.subject: Find the parents of Pablo Armando Lerena
commits.body:
An Argentine army ficha de enrolamiento (FamilySearch image group #112342450,
image 665 of 1,119, volume "Cajon 985 (Lera)") reads:
  Clase de 1882 / LERENA - Pablo Armando
  hijo de Juan Carlos Lerena y de Maria Lerena
  Nacido en Rosario de Santa Fe
  Oficina enroladora de Capetown
The class of 1882, the birthplace, and the Cape Town enrolling office were all
already known from his own passport and death certificate. Corroborated from
outside Argentina: his eldest son, named in the 1950 estate, was Ricardo Juan
Carlos Lerena, b. 6 Jan 1920.
The record had been found in the previous round and written off as "probably not
him" on four objections. Three were artefacts of a machine index that dropped
"Pablo", moved him to Salta, wrote Lerena as Lorena, and made a surname "Serena"
out of the printed word SERIE. Only the image could tell them apart.
- direct-line.tsv: generation 0 added, documented
- lerena-register.tsv: the false candidate resolved, Juan Carlos added (117 people)
- enrolment-card-1908.tsv: the card transcribed field by field
- notes/the-cape-town-enrolment-card.md, notes/findings.md
- site: new /enrolment-card/ page; home, line, open questions and sources rewritten
- tools/build-people.py: the register-to-JSON generator, saved rather than ad hoc
- register.astro now generates its table from people.json instead of hard-coded rows
Still open and said plainly: Maria is written with her husband's surname, so
whether she was a Lerena by birth is undecided; and the Rosario baptism index
still holds no Lerena at all for 1881-1883.

commits.subject: Cordoba opened, and an Armando born 1882 with a mother named Lerena
commits.body:
Four of the five moved; two are recorded as not reached.
2. The 1895 census re-run under Llerena and Lorena CONFIRMS rather than
overturns. No Llerena in Santa Fe in 1895, and the Lorena entries at
Rosario are Spanish-born - a different family, exactly as suspected at
Cayasta.
1. CORDOBA, never searched, has a Llerena family. Bartolome was born
there in 1824, so the province mattered and had been overlooked. At
Cordoba Cathedral: Francisco Llerena m. Rafaela Daraz, their son
Baldomero b.1851 m. Margarita Correas in 1876; also Rafael Llerena m.
Rosario Moyano, Lucrecia, Amalia. Bartolome belongs to Francisco and
Rafael's generation, plausibly a brother. No Pablo and no Armando among
them.
And then, in the Argentine military records: ARMAND[O] LORENA, born 1882,
birthplace ROSARIO de Lerma in Salta, father Juan Carlos Lorena Serena,
MOTHER MARIA LERENA. Born 1882; named Armando, a name shown to be rare;
born at a place called Rosario; mother surnamed Lerena, which is exactly
the mother's-surname hypothesis this archive has carried for days; and in
the military records where a clase 1882 man belongs.
The objections are serious and are not softened: Rosario de Lerma is in
SALTA, 1,400km from Rosario de Santa Fe, and the passport names the
province; the forename is Armando not Pablo Armando; the surname is
Lorena; and FamilySearch states the record was machine-indexed. Probably
not him - worth opening anyway, and the original is linked.
4. Carlos Gustavo Lerena b.1915 is not in FamilySearch's Argentine
records at all; that thread needs foreign-ministry staff lists.
3 and 5 - Trinidad's six brothers and a full-text sweep - were not
reached, and the notes say so.
Register now 116 people; 161 pages build clean, with a page for each new
person and place.

commits.subject: A page for every person and place; architecture aligned with the Defranceski archive
commits.body:
Five things, all done.
1. DIFFED AGAINST THE DEFRANCESKI SITE rather than working from memory.
The stylesheet turns out to be byte-identical apart from one block I
added, so the branding was already aligned. What differed was
ARCHITECTURE: that archive has /people/, /places/ and per-person pages
built from JSON data with dynamic routes. This adopts the same pattern.
2. A PAGE PER PERSON. All 104, at /people/<slug>/, generated from
data/lerena-register.tsv via src/data/people.json so they cannot drift
from the register. Each carries the full record - born, birthplace,
nationality, occupation, where found, source - a status chip, what is
known, a card through to the place, and the others found in that same
place. Connected and excluded people get an explanatory note rather than
a bare label.
3. EVERY NAME LINKED. All 104 names in the register now link through to
their person page. A searchable /people/ index lists everyone with live
filtering.
4. A PLACES INDEX. 23 places at /places/<slug>/, each listing everyone of
the name found there with their source. The index opens by saying what
the geography actually shows: the surname clusters in the River Plate and
at Trinidad in Flores, while ROSARIO - the one place the family itself
names - is the thinnest of all.
5. CONTENT BROUGHT CURRENT. The Taylors page now carries the eight-year
gap and the two candidate ships, with the caveat that Taylor is among the
commonest English surnames and this is a candidate not an
identification. The searched page carries the full-text search finding -
that Argentine records ARE in the corpus, that the coverage seen is Santa
Fe La Capital rather than Rosario, and that no sweep has yet been run.
145 pages build clean. All internal page links verified against the built
output; none broken.

commits.subject: The eight-year gap narrowed to two named ships
commits.body:
Pursuing point 4 of the five. No Mary Taylor of her age left Britain for
South Africa at all - the outward lists 1890-1960, searched on forename,
age and destination, return zero.
But the index often carries no forename. Dropping it and filtering on
surname, age and destination produces two candidates in exactly the right
window:
  MISS Taylor, 19, single, DOMESTIC - Southampton to Cape, 9 September
  1903, ship Harlech Castle - TNA BT 27/0420 p.68 image 0004F
  MISS Taylor, 19, single - Southampton to Cape, 9 April 1904, ship
  Walmer Castle - TNA BT 27/0448
Mary Septima was born 17 September 1884, so on 9 September 1903 she was
eight days short of nineteen, and the manifest says nineteen. The
occupation fits the life: a pupil teacher at sixteen in a cab driver's
household of ten children, at a moment when the Cape was actively
recruiting British domestic servants with assisted passage. That would
put her in Cape Town about two years before Roque was born there.
Recorded as a CANDIDATE, not an identification. Taylor is among the
commonest English surnames and "Miss Taylor, 19" will have sailed for the
Cape many times. The original images would show the forename - the
transcripts read perfectly but findmypast's tile viewer would not render
in this browser, so the images remain unopened. Two minutes' work in an
ordinary browser, and both references are recorded.

commits.subject: The five-point push: full-text confirmed live, and the Gilberto family joins up
commits.body:
1. FULL-TEXT SEARCH. The instrument works and the key question is
answered: Argentine records ARE in the corpus - "Santa Fe, La Capital.
Religious Marriage Records 1879-1882" and "1882-1883" are full-text
searchable. This is the first tool in the project that reads handwriting
nobody has indexed. Two caveats recorded: the coverage seen is Santa Fe
LA CAPITAL, not Rosario, a different city; and the React search box drops
programmatic input and swallows about half the submissions, so queries
must be typed and verified one at a time. No Lerena hit yet, but nothing
like a sweep has been run. Stays open as a live lead.
2. MILITARY RECORDS. No Pablo Armando of any surname born 1880-84 in the
Argentine records, and no military entry for the surname. The passport's
Guardia Nacional service still has to come from the Archivo General del
Ejercito, and that letter is with them.
5. THE GILBERTO THREAD - the find of the round. A Buenos Aires marriage
register gives Carlos LERENA, born 1884 MONTEVIDEO, parents Alberto
(almost certainly Gilberto) Lerena and JULIA SALVANACH, married ROSA
MARIA EPPENS. That identifies the CEMLA couple "Carlos Lerena 41
Uruguayan" and "Rosa M. E. Lerena 39 Argentine" arriving Buenos Aires
from Montevideo on 27 May 1926 - two entirely independent sources
describing the same couple.
Also new: Avelino Carlos Lerena, baptised 12 March 1904 at Mendoza,
parents Carlos Lerena and Adela Camiglia - giving a birth and a parentage
to the Avelino Carlos who crossed to New York in 1940 and Rio in 1949 and
1953.
The Stud Book family is now a documented multi-generation Argentine
family rather than a name recurring in indexes - and it is the family
whose forename stock the South African branch kept using. Still no
connection to Pablo Armando.
3 and 4 not advanced this round and said so: the rest of the 1869 Rosario
census, and the 1901-1909 gap in Mary Septima's life. They remain the two
most tractable jobs left.
Register regenerated to 104 people; home page count updated.

commits.subject: Site brought up to date: register searchable, stale claims cleared, sources linked
commits.body:
The site had fallen two days behind the research. This closes the gap.
REGISTER now generated straight from data/lerena-register.tsv so the two
cannot drift apart, and carries a live search box over all 100 people -
name, place, year, source or status, so "Trinidad", "Gilberto", "1882",
"CEMLA" or "connected" all work. Counts shown honestly: 5 connected, 7
excluded, 88 unplaced.
STALE CLAIMS CLEARED. The direct-line page still said its "present
emptiness is the most accurate thing on the site" and described the line
as a skeleton - untrue for days. Its dek, intro and "what is still
missing" section are rewritten: the descent is closed and documented, the
Rosario baptism route is exhausted rather than promising, and the hope
now rests on the three letters with archives. The home page said
"fourteen consecutive years of Rosario baptisms"; it now says
seventy-eight letter-bands across 1881-83, and adds the register as a
seventh number. The Argentina page said the baptism "would name them, and
it is now an exact target" - corrected to say the route is exhausted.
ARGENTINA PAGE brought current with three new sections: the registers
searched to the end; the surname finally found in Rosario (Bartolome
Llerena 1869, and the two Santa Rosa de Lima families of 1903 and 1918),
with the honest deflation that Bartolome is a lodger and a day labourer;
and "Which Rosario?", on the Colonia ambiguity.
SOURCES had zero links. It now carries every film, collection, outside
database and archive actually used, each linked, in four tables - with
the note that every archive address was verified from the institution's
own contact page and none invented.
All internal links checked against the built output; none broken.

commits.subject: Which Rosario? Gabino corrected, and a third Uruguayan cluster at Colonia
commits.body:
Opened Gabino L. Llerena's marriage record. His "Rosario" is ROSARIO,
COLONIA, URUGUAY - not Rosario de Santa Fe. Every other person named on
the record is Uruguayan: Solis Grande, Maldonado, Punta de Carretas,
Cordon Montevideo, Monte Video. Flagging him last night as a Rosario-born
Llerena linking the two countries was wrong, and is corrected on the
register before it hardened into a claim.
Uruguay has its own Rosario. Any Uruguayan record naming Rosario means
the Colonia town unless it says otherwise - and given how much of this
family's evidence runs through Uruguay, that ambiguity has been sitting
unremarked in the middle of the problem.
The hypothesis it raises is recorded and is weak: if the family's memory
of "Rosario" came down through a Uruguayan branch, the town could be the
wrong one entirely. But the passport says "Rosario de Santa Fe", naming
the province, in his own document. It would take far more than an
ambiguity to overturn that.
The search also produced a third Uruguayan Llerena cluster, after
Trinidad in Flores and Montevideo - this one in COLONIA: Tomas Llerena m.
Maria Morales; Pedro Llerena m. Sofia Clavijo, whose daughter Susana was
born 1884 - exactly the generation that could have fathered a son in
1882; Maria Llerena m. Antonio Medero; Ramon and Gabino at Rosario,
Colonia.
Still no Pablo Armando. Uruguay has now been searched across civil
registration, church records and baptisms in Flores, Montevideo, San Jose
and Colonia, and he is in none of it.

commits.subject: The 1869 census image read - and my household reading corrected
commits.body:
Opened film 004331984 image 86, Rosario Seccion 2a, and panned and
magnified it until every field was legible.
My "household" reading last night was wrong and is corrected rather than
quietly dropped. There is no Lerena family on that page. Every line
carries its own number and the twelve people are of a dozen different
surnames - washerwomen, a laundress, day labourers, a peon, a carpenter,
a Spanish shopkeeper. It is a list of individuals at one address, a
conventillo or lodgings. The Lorena and Lorona entries I grouped with
Bartolome are elsewhere in the census entirely; the line I expected to be
a Lorena is Vachalo.
So there is no Lerena family in Rosario in 1869. There is one man:
Bartolome LLERENA, 45, married, Argentine, born Cordoba, JORNALERO,
Rosario Seccion 2a.
He is still the only person of this surname found in Rosario before 1882,
which is worth having. But he lodges among strangers with no wife or
children beside him though recorded married; he is a day labourer, not a
horseman or a man of property; and the surname on the page reads Llerena
with the Castilian double L.
Weaker than it looked last night, and still the best pre-1882 Rosario
evidence there is. Register corrected accordingly.

commits.subject: The 1869 census of Rosario: the surname in the city before he was born
commits.body:
Working Santa Rosa de Lima produced the best lead in days. The 1869
National Census shows people of this surname living in ROSARIO - the
first time this archive has found any, anywhere in the city, before 1882.
Bartolome LLERENA, born 1824 in Cordoba. And alongside him a household
indexed as "Lorena": Agustin (b.1829) with children born at Cordoba
between 1853 and 1868 - Guillermo, Geronima, Mercedes, Feliz, Maria -
plus Luis and Jose Lorona. A family that moved Cordoba to Rosario in the
1860s.
Bartolome would be 58 in 1882 and Agustin 53 - either old enough to be
Pablo Armando's grandfather - and the children born in the 1850s are
exactly the right age to be his parents.
The objection is stated rather than buried: Lorena is a real and separate
surname, and the index may simply be right. But the same small group is
indexed under THREE spellings - Llerena, Lorena, Lorona - which is what
an indexer does with one difficult hand; the names differ by a single
letter; and this project has already watched Belmonte read as Sarmiento
and Laurini read as Larena. Recorded as a hypothesis, not a finding.
It is settleable with one image. The 1869 schedules are digitised; the
hand will show whether it is Lerena, Lorena or Llerena, and the schedule
gives the household structure the index strips away. That is now the most
valuable single unexamined document in the Argentine work.
Two more threads: Gabino L. Llerena, a groom in the Uruguayan church
records whose BIRTHPLACE IS GIVEN AS ROSARIO; and Camilo Llerena, 1869
census at Nogoya, Entre Rios, born 1842 in Santa Fe - the province of the
Gualeguaychu Larena kindred.
All nine added to the register.

commits.subject: Libro 8 answered: no Lerena marriage at Rosario 1868-1891
commits.body:
Libro 8 is a different film - Matrimonios 1868-1884, DGS 4531040: sixteen
years, some 3,000 marriages, 500-odd images. Rather than page it, used
the searchable index - but only after proving the index covers those
years. A control search returns cathedral marriages of 1874, 1875 and
1876 with full parentage. The 1868-1884 Rosario marriages are indexed, so
the null is about the record and not the coverage.
There is no Lerena marriage at Rosario cathedral in Libro 8. Searching
LERENA at Rosario returns 38 records and not one is a marriage before
1900. Taken with the act-by-act read of Libro 9's 1884, there is no
Lerena marriage at Rosario across 1868-1891.
The difference in standard is stated rather than glossed: Libro 9's 1884
was read act by act; Libro 8 rests on the index. The control proves the
index is good, but an index carries gaps and mis-spellings in a way a
page-by-page read does not.
And the search produced the first Lerenas ever found living in Rosario
itself, both at Santa Rosa de Lima - the parish that only opened in 1888:
Luis Llerena m. Clementina Baranda, son Luis Alejandro baptised 1903; and
Manuela Lerena m. Diego Roman, daughter Carmen baptised 1918. Neither can
be his parents, both being a generation too late, but they are the first
evidence the surname existed in the city at all. Added to the register.

commits.subject: All of Libro 9's 1884 read: one Lavena, no Sarmiento, no Lerena
commits.body:
Closes the residual left this morning. 8 June to 31 December 1884 has now
been read act by act through the Image Index panel, running on into 2
January 1885 to be sure of the boundary - roughly two hundred marriages,
each with both parties and all four parents.
Libro 9 begins in June 1884: the film's title card reads 1884-1888,
PRINCIPIO is at image 4, the register starts at image 5, and the earliest
dated act in the book is 8 June 1884. January to May 1884 is not in this
book at all - it belongs to Libro 8, a different film. The index entry
said "Libro 9", so the relevant year is covered end to end.
In the whole year, exactly one marriage involves any of Sarmiento,
Larena, Lavena, Lerena or Llerena: Vicente LAVENA x Angela BELMONTE, 3
August 1884. No Sarmiento anywhere in 1884. No Lerena anywhere in 1884.

commits.subject: Folio 20 settled: the candidate is Vicente LAVENA, not a Lerena
commits.body:
Reached it with the index-panel method - single-image mode via a
thumbnail click, then stepping with the viewer's arrows and extracting
the Image Index panel as text at each image.
Read act by act, 8 June to 29 September 1884 at Rosario cathedral, about
ninety marriages. Exactly one hit:
  Vicente LAVENA, 26, b.1858, son of Miguel Lavena and Lucia Lavena,
  married Angela BELMONTE, 21, b.1863, daughter of Pascual Belmonte and
  Maria Cozsi, on 3 August 1884 at the Catedral de Nuestra Senora del
  Rosario.
The index line read "Larena/Lavena V x Sarmiento A, folio 20". The first
surname is LAVENA, confirmed from the register. V is Vicente, A is
Angela - both initials match in order, and it is the only L-surname
marriage in three and a half months.
The "Sarmiento" was my own misreading of BELMONTE in the low-resolution
index image. Recorded rather than dropped, because it is why this
candidate survived as a lead for two days.
This closes the last open candidate for a Lerena marriage at Rosario.
Vicente Lavena was Italian, which fits the Lavenas of Rosario exactly.
There is no Lerena marriage at Rosario cathedral in 1884.
Residual stated: October to December 1884 unscanned. The candidate is
identified so the item is closed, but four or five more arrow-steps would
make the year airtight.

commits.subject: Method: the Rosario registers can be read as TEXT - and a correction
commits.body:
David challenged my claim that settling the 1884 marriage candidate
needed the Chrome extension. He was right and the claim was wrong twice
over. The viewer has its own zoom, so magnification never depended on the
screenshot tool's inability to crop. And far more importantly, the
handwriting does not need to be read at all.
Every image in these films carries an "Image Index" panel that is HTML
text, not an image. For a marriage act it gives both parties, their ages,
and BOTH SETS OF PARENTS, plus date and parish - the entire genealogical
content of the act - pullable with a one-line querySelector.
That turns the Rosario marriage registers into a database. It applies to
the whole series and would have saved much of the baptism sweep had it
been understood earlier.
Proved on 8 June - 8 July 1884 at the Cathedral: about fifteen marriages
captured in full with all four parents each, tabulated in the note. No
Sarmiento and no L-surname of interest in that stretch.
Still open: the candidate at Libro 9 folio 20 was not reached. The
viewer's grid/single-mode switching keeps resetting position and the
index panel materialises on some loads and not others - a mechanical
obstacle, not a research one. About twenty images cover all of 1884, six
marriages each. Practical notes recorded: enter single-image mode by
clicking a thumbnail, then step with the arrows; navigating by number or
?i= URL bounces back to the grid.

commits.subject: Cayasta retracted as a transcription artefact; the Gualeguaychu kindred recorded
commits.body:
Looked properly at Cayasta and it does not survive. The village was an
Italian agricultural colony - its register runs Laurini x5, Lauron,
Castelarin, Masorini, Panluzzi, Gaetta, Salvaserra - and the same mother
is transcribed "Ines Azela" for one child and "Ines Raiela" for the
other, which is what an indexer does with a name they cannot read.
"Larena" there is almost certainly an Italian surname mis-rendered, and
the apparent Larena/Lerena cluster is the index mangling two different
Italian families. The register entry is corrected to EXCLUDED and the
claim retracted in findings.md rather than quietly deleted.
The same search did turn up something real: a four-generation LARENA
family at Gualeguaychu, Entre Rios - Juan Larena m. Petrona Lopez, Juan
Antonio b.1837, Victorino Severo b.1878, Vicente Antonio, Tito Gregorio,
Juan Jose, Aureliano Emiliano - and a ROQUE LARENA, born 1881, married
Florencia Calixta Ramos. Gualeguaychu is also the town of Juan Pablo
Lerena, baptised 1891, one of only two Lerena baptisms indexed in all
Argentina.
Roque is why it caught the eye - the name Pablo Armando gave his eldest
son, on a man born within a year of him. But there is NO Pablo Larena and
NO Armando Larena anywhere in Entre Rios; four generations and neither of
our names in any of them. And Gualeguaychu is on the far side of the
country from Rosario. Recorded on the register as unplaced - a candidate
for elimination, not a discovery.

commits.subject: Sweep closed; a Larena household found at Cayasta, Santa Fe
commits.body:
Records that the 1881-1883 sweep is finished and should not be restarted,
and states the one film item still open: the 1884 marriage candidate
Larena/Lavena x Sarmiento, Libro 9 folio 20, DGS 4531041.
Short of reading that page, today established two things about it.
Lavena is a real and well-documented Rosario surname - an Italian family,
Francisco Lavena born Italy 1880, in Rosario at the 1895 census, children
baptised at San Jose and the Cathedral 1900-1915. And no Larena or Lerena
marriage appears anywhere in Rosario's indexed records. On balance the
entry reads Lavena - recorded as a judgement, not a reading, because the
page still has not been seen.
Why it was not settled: the register is handwriting and the in-app
browser cannot crop to a region, only return full screenshots, at which
scale a 19th-century marginal folio number is illegible. The Chrome
extension can region-zoom and is disconnected.
The find of the day is incidental: ANTONIO LARENA of Cayasta, Garay,
Santa Fe, with children Maria (1890) and Carmela (1892) by Ines
Azela/Raiela - and Cayasta is the same village as the only Lerena baptism
indexed in all Argentina, Leon Jose Lerena 1892, father Jose. Two
households of a rare surname in one small village in the same two years,
and the first time the name has been found SETTLED in Santa Fe province
rather than passing through it. Added to the register.

commits.subject: Letter sent to the IISH, Amsterdam: Argentine anarchist press and Ley 4144
commits.body:
Sent to ask@iisg.nl, Gmail msg 1a084e17877f1a41. Address verified from
the Institute's own contact page - ask@ is collections and reading room,
info@ is general, communicatie@ is press.
Amsterdam is the same question as the AGN's by an easier door: the AGN
has no email and its portal is account-gated, while the IISH answers
email and holds a major collection of Latin American anarchist material.
The anarchist press named names - arrests, imprisonments and deportations
of individual militants, often in lists.
Asks four things: the 1902-06 Argentine anarchist periodicals and whether
any are text-searchable; Rosario and Santa Fe labour papers; FORA and
prisoners' committee records naming those deported under Ley 4144; and
whether a surname search can be done remotely or needs a reader in
Amsterdam.
The letter translates the family story rather than repeating it - the
Argentine communist party dates from 1918 and he left in 1903-05 - and
explains the foreign-born point that makes Ley 4144 bear on the birth
question. It asserts nothing about the Institute's holdings; every point
is put as a question.

commits.subject: Pin down the AGN submission route; note the Cancilleria form is CAPTCHA-gated
commits.body:
Records exactly where the AGN enquiry has to go: register at
agnbicentenario.mininterior.gob.ar/web/ingresar - a passport suffices for
foreigners - then submit at the consultas dashboard. The AGN publishes no
email address anywhere; the portal is the only remote channel, and no
address has been invented to make the request look finished.
Also records, for the avoidance of doubt, that the Cancilleria's own web
form sits behind Google reCAPTCHA and so could not have been submitted
from here either. Their published email was the only route open - which
is precisely what they offer it for.

commits.subject: Cancilleria letter sent; AGN expulsion request written but blocked
commits.body:
Sent to the Archivo Historico de Cancilleria, archivo@cancilleria.gob.ar,
Gmail msg 1a084cbef3384599. The address was verified from the
Cancilleria's own contact page - text and a live mailto link - not
guessed and not taken from a search summary.
It asks for the matricula consular of the Cape Town consulate 1930-50,
the file behind the 1940 passport and above all WHAT HE PRODUCED TO PROVE
ARGENTINE NATIONALITY and whether it names his parents, the consular
correspondence, and - flagged as minor and explicitly not worth staff
time - whether he ever held a consular appointment. That last question
puts the family's Consul General tradition to the one body that could
settle it.
The expulsion request is written but NOT sent, for two reasons recorded
plainly:
1. A correction to the brief: these are not army records. The letter
   already with the Archivo General del Ejercito asks for his libreta de
   enrolamiento - military enrolment, a different thing. Ley 4144
   expulsions were run by the Ministerio del Interior and the police, and
   the files sit with the Archivo General de la Nacion.
2. The AGN has closed its email channel. Its only remote route is a
   portal requiring a registered account, and no AGN email is published
   anywhere. None has been invented. The full Spanish text is in
   requests/agn-ley-4144-expulsiones.md ready to paste.
Alternatives noted: the Archivo Historico de la Provincia de Santa Fe and
provincial police holdings, and the International Institute of Social
History in Amsterdam, which holds the Argentine anarchist collections
including La Protesta and does answer email.
Adds a "Letters written to archives" table to /searched/ so the
correspondence is on the record with its status.

commits.subject: Spain tested: no Pablo Lerena in 1882 - and no Armando Lerena, ever
commits.body:
The fourth and last candidate birthplace. No Pablo Lerena born 1882 in
Spain; the whole country yields one of the right generation, Pablo
Timoteo Lerena Munoz, born 1878 at Atienza in Guadalajara, who married
there and stayed.
The finding that actually discriminates is the other one: THERE IS NO
ARMANDO LERENA IN SPAIN AT ALL, in any collection, in any century. Every
hit is fuzzy noise. Yet Armando is the name this family keeps across four
generations and two continents - Pablo Armando, his son Roque Luis
Armando, Anton Armando of the 1980 divorce and 2013 estate, and Gregorio
Armando Lerena marrying at Flores in Uruguay in 1930.
Armando is a Rio de la Plata name, not a Spanish peninsular one of the
1880s; it entered Spanish through Italian influence, which is the
demographic signature of Buenos Aires, Rosario and Montevideo in exactly
that period. Across three entire years of the Rosario index there were
two Armandos - rare, but present. Across four centuries of indexed
Spanish records, none.
Of every test run in this archive, this is the FIRST that argues for one
origin over another rather than merely failing to find him.
Supporting: Spanish Lerenas are scattered rather than a kindred, and in
most cases Lerena is the second maternal surname - nothing like the six
brothers at Trinidad. And Spanish practice gives two surnames where his
passport carries one.
Honest limit recorded: Spanish parish registers are enormous and only
patchily indexed, so this is a weaker negative than the Uruguayan test.
Adds a name-page footnote: Llerena is a town in Badajoz and the surname
is toponymic from it, which is why both spellings have had to be run in
every search.

commits.subject: Uruguayan civil registration tested: no Pablo Armando, and a bigger kindred
commits.body:
Runs the successor test to the Rosario sweep. Uruguay was chosen for a
specific reason: its civil registration began in 1879, three years before
his stated birth and seven before Santa Fe's - the absence of early civil
registration being exactly what makes the Argentine trail dead-end.
Result: there is NO Pablo Armando Lerena in the Uruguayan records at all,
and no Pablo Lerena born in 1882. The complete list of Pablo Lerenas in
Uruguay is four people, none of them ours. Nor is there a Pablo Armando
of any surname born in Uruguay in 1882.
The control holds: the index DOES contain Lerena births from this exact
window, including Maria Luisa Lerena born 19 July 1882 in Rio Negro. So
this is an absence in the record, not a hole in the coverage. It remains
an index rather than the registers themselves, so it substantially
weakens the Uruguayan-birth idea without finally killing it - and the
site says exactly that.
What it gave instead is a much enlarged Uruguayan kindred, clustering at
Flores and Montevideo just as the baptisms predicted - including Gregorio
ARMANDO Lerena, marrying at Flores in 1930, the only Armando Lerena in
any of these records.
Three of four candidate birthplaces are now tested and failed. Spain is
untested, and is where the surname is most numerous in absolute terms,
concentrated on Logrono - exactly as the CEMLA arrivals showed.
Also adds the estate conversion at David's request. The Six numbers panel
and the estate page now carry it, with the currency named correctly as
South African pounds (at par with sterling in 1950) and both measures
given: about 500,000 pounds by retail prices, about 1.4 million measured
against earnings. The 26 pounds owed for carrots is about 830 today.

commits.subject: Fix the roadmap note left stale by the completed sweep
commits.body:
Route 5's follow-on note still told the reader that 1881 and 1883 were
the cheapest unrun test. They have just been run. Corrected to say the
Rosario baptism route is exhausted, and to name Uruguayan civil
registration for 1882 as the cheapest untried test instead.

commits.subject: THE SWEEP IS FINISHED: 1881, 1882 and 1883, all 26 sections, no Pablo Armando
commits.body:
Completes N through Z for both neighbouring years. All twenty-six letter
sections of the Rosario cathedral baptism index are now read for 1881,
1882 and 1883 alike, looking for the given name Pablo Armando under any
surname whatsoever. He is in none of them. Roughly two hundred
image-reads across a 718-image film.
Several sections are tiny, and the numbers matter because they show how
thin this register is at the edges of the alphabet: Q has TEN entries in
the whole of 1881 and thirteen in 1883; W has exactly ONE entry in each
year; Y's entire section is a single line for 1900; Ll has no 1881
entries at all; and there is no X section.
More than twenty near misses across the three years, all excluded. Only
TWO Armandos exist in all three years - Ronillon Armando Juan and Funes
Armando, both 1882. That is what makes the null mean something: the
method plainly catches the name when it is there.
What this establishes: no child named Pablo Armando was baptised at the
only parish in Rosario across a three-year window centred on his stated
birth date. What it does NOT establish: that he was not born there - he
may have been baptised under a different given name, outside the window,
or not at all.
The Rosario baptism route is now EXHAUSTED rather than merely
unsuccessful, and the site says so. Weight shifts to evidence gathered
while the sweep ran: his Argentine nationality proved from outside the
family by 1911; the Uruguayan kindred at Trinidad, Flores; and the
political-refugee story, which if it means expulsion under the Ley de
Residencia would require him to be foreign-born - explaining this null
completely. The cheapest untried test is now Uruguayan civil
registration for 1882, which began in 1879.

commits.subject: 1881/1883 sweep: fourteen of twenty-six sections complete
commits.body:
A B C D E F G H I J K L Ll M are now read for BOTH 1881 and 1883 - twenty
eight bands - and Pablo Armando is in none of them. F being clear extends
the Fernandez null to both neighbouring years.
Two sections turn out to be nearly empty, which is worth recording rather
than glossing:
- K has FOUR entries in the whole of 1881 and TWO in 1883. It is a tiny
  section of Irish and German surnames, and it jumps Libro 24 (1881)
  straight to Libro 26 (1883) - which is exactly why the 1882 sweep found
  nothing there.
- Ll has NO 1881 ENTRIES AT ALL, and three in 1883. Still no Llerena.
Near misses logged: Galavotto/Pablo D. Rosa, a bare Pablo in H and
another in I, Lopez/Pablo, Lamberti/Atilio Pablo Juan, Moron/Juan Pablo
(1881); Ledesma/Juan Pablo, Leguisamon/Pedro Pablo, Lopez/Pablo Gregorio,
Luraschi/Santos Pablo, Medina/Pablo Mauricio, Mendieta/Jose Pablo (1883).
A practical discovery worth keeping: SOME FRAMES OF THIS FILM ARE
DUPLICATES of their neighbour - image 418 returns 417's opening, 424
returns 423's. The folio sequences prove it, running unbroken across the
images either side with no room for an extra opening between. That is
also the likeliest explanation of the 718-versus-655 image count between
the two viewer states. Coverage is therefore verified by FOLIO
CONTINUITY, never by image number alone, and the coverage file now says
so explicitly.
Thirteen sections remain: N O P Q R S T U V W X Y Z.

commits.subject: Censuses: William Taylor was a retired cavalry sergeant
commits.body:
1891 and 1901 censuses of Northam, Devon, read on findmypast.
The correction is the find. This archive carried William Taylor - Mary
Septima's father - as a "coachman", from the MyHeritage tree. The 1891
enumerator writes his occupation as "Cab driver retired sergt p cavaloy":
cab driver, retired sergeant, CAVALRY. By 1901 he is a widower of North
Street, Northam, and an army pensioner. His eldest son drove a cab beside
him; his second son was a footman.
So horses stand behind BOTH sides of this marriage. Pablo Armando's whole
story is horses - trainer, breeder, stables, four generations of jockeys
after him - and it turns out the woman he married came from a cavalryman
who drove a cab. That proves nothing and explains nothing, but the
archive had been treating Mary Septima as the ordinary English half of
the story and that was plainly wrong.
Also from the censuses:
- The pupil-teacher finding is independently corroborated. The 1901
  census (31 Mar) records "Mary Taylor, daughter, 16, SCHOOL TEACHER,
  born Northam"; the Western Times printed the diocesan exam results on
  4 April. Two unrelated sources, four days apart.
- Her mother Mary Ann Hellen is recorded as born LONDON, MIDDLESEX, not
  Devon, though Brayley is a north Devon surname. Unresolved.
- An anomaly, recorded not explained: Mary Septima is ABSENT from the
  1891 census. She should be six in that household. No Mary Taylor born
  1883-85 anywhere in Devon fits. Needs checking against the image.
Full households in data/taylor-censuses.tsv; write-up in
notes/the-taylors-had-horses-too.md; Taylors page updated.

commits.subject: Newspapers cracked: Mary Septima was a pupil teacher at Northam
commits.body:
Retried the newspaper search - the path is /search-newspapers/results and
the OCR hides behind an Articles button on the image viewer.
Western Times, 4 April 1901 p.7, and North Devon Herald, 11 April 1901
p.2, both print the Exeter Diocesan Board of Education examination
results. Under Set II - monitors over sixteen and pupil teachers in their
FIRST YEAR, 88 examined - she is in Class III: "Mary Septima Taylor, 16,
Northam." She was training to teach in her own village school.
This is the first thing the archive knows about her that is not a date,
and it exposes the real gap: a pupil teacher at Northam in April 1901,
and "Mrs Lerena" crossing from Cape Town to Southampton with a
three-year-old son by February 1909. Eight years, and the whole distance
between a Devon parish school and an Argentine horseman's household at
the Cape. That is now the largest answerable hole in the story.
Also closed off an avenue: a newspaper search on "Lerena" returns 1,344
articles that are almost entirely OCR noise - Nissan Serena adverts
misread as LERENA. Nothing of ours. Recorded so it is not retried.

commits.subject: findmypast: Argentine nationality corroborated from outside the family
commits.body:
David opened a trial subscription. Four findings.
1. NATIONALITY. Mary Septima's declared nationality on British passenger
manifests: ENGLISH in Feb 1909, ARGENTINE in May 1935. She was born and
baptised at Northam, Devon. Under the law of the period a British woman
took her husband's nationality on marriage, and they married in September
1911 - between the two voyages. A ship's purser in 1935, with no interest
in this family, wrote down that a Devon woman was Argentine. That is
independent corroboration that Pablo Armando held Argentine nationality
by 1911, not merely by 1940. It does not settle where he was born.
2. The 1909 manifest lists on CONSECUTIVE LINES: Mrs M T Lerena (English)
and Mast. L Lerena, a boy, British Colonial. Roque LUIS Armando was born
at Cape Town in Nov 1905, so he was three, and the 1950 estate calls him
"LOUIS Lerena". So she was travelling as Mrs Lerena with their son two
years before the marriage - the same pattern already documented for
Roque, and the basis of the mother's-surname theory.
3. In 1935 she arrived Southampton on 20 May, address "C/O DALLING, FORE
ST, NORTHAM" - her elder sister Isabella "Edie" Taylor married a Dalling.
She sailed home 28 June and died 15 November. A five-week visit home.
4. Carlos Gustavo Lerena, b.1915, ARGENTINE, occupation DIPLOMATIC,
arrived London 1958 en route to a posting in Iran, with a son named
Carlos GILBERTO. Not our man and no proof of the Consul General story,
but it shows Lerenas did serve in Argentine diplomacy, and it is the
third independent appearance of the Carlos-and-Gilberto pairing.
Also: only eight Lerenas ever arrived in Britain and only two ever left;
Pablo Armando is not among them. Juanita Ramona Lerena b. 16 Jun 1937,
ballet teacher, arrived 1957 to Westward Ho, the village next to Northam.

commits.subject: findmypast: Mary Septima's 1935 voyage, and the Uruguayan nest at Trinidad
commits.body:
David logged the session into findmypast. Result rows are free; transcripts
are paywalled and were NOT purchased. Everything below is index-level.
*** THE BEST NEW LEAD ***
Mary Septima Lerena, born 1885, appears TWICE in 1935 - the year she died
(15 Nov 1935). Incoming to Great Britain (TNA BT26/1079/00247, findmypast
BT26/10691490) and leaving the UK for Cape, South Africa (TNA
BT27/1433/00/0068). She sailed to England and back in the last year of her
life. The OUTWARD list names everyone in the party, so it may put Pablo
Armando on a dated ship with his age, occupation, UK address and declared
nationality - a document type we have never had for him. Written up in
notes/mary-septima-1935-voyage.md.
Also: two Lerenas, "L" and "M T", arriving in Britain together in 1909 on
one page (TNA BT26/398/00161). Pablo Armando married Mary Septima in 1911
and the family story is that they met on a ship.
*** THE URUGUAYAN NEST ***
Uruguay Baptisms 1750-1900 returns 33 Lerena rows with parents named.
Eleven children are baptised in ONE small town - Trinidad, department of
Flores - in the 1870s, to SIX different fathers (Bernabe, Vitalino, Ysaac,
Cipriano, Fermin, Luis). Six men of a rare surname in one town in a few
years are almost certainly brothers. That is the founding kindred, and it
explains why Uruguay has the highest density of the name on earth.
It also confirms the Gilberto family independently: Carlos Augusto Federico
Lerena, b.1883 Montevideo, father Gilberto, mother Julia - the same child
found as "Carlos A., 11, born Uruguay" in Gilberto Lerena's Buenos Aires
household at the 1895 Argentine census.
But: there is NO Pablo and NO Armando in the Uruguayan set, and only TWO
Lerena baptisms in the whole Argentina Baptisms 1645-1930 index - one at
Gualeguaychu 1891, one at Cayasta, SANTA FE, 1892, father Jose. Written up
in notes/trinidad-flores.md, with the next step: Uruguayan CIVIL
registration began in 1879, so a Uruguayan birth in 1882 should be
civilly recorded.

commits.subject: 1881/1883 sweep: A-E done. SA estates index. Film structure resolved
commits.body:
Sweep: A, B, C, D and E are now complete for both 1881 and 1883 - ten
bands, no Pablo Armando. New near misses: Carara/Pablo (1881 f.146),
Dias/Jose Pablo (1883 f.92).
Resolves the image-numbering confusion properly rather than working
around it. The film carries TWO rolls. Roll 29 ends at image 171 with a
title card for Volume A-D and "continua en el proximo rollo"; images
172-178 are leader and title cards; the volume resumes at 179 marked
"continuacion". The 655-image waypoint view OMITS that roll-30
continuation - the tail of C and the whole of D - which is exactly the
63-image difference. D exists only in the 718-image film view. Both
coverage files now say which view their numbers came from, and record
the Libro/folio spans, which are stable across views.
New source from David: ancestors.co.za deceased estates, 1994-2023.
Gives death years not previously held for Ricardo Juan Carlos (1996),
Pierre Frederick (2000), Paul Raymond (2001), Anton Armando (2013) and
Roberto Juan Roque (2022), and a full name - Doreen May - for the
"Doreen" of the family chart. Robert Paul Lerena 1950 appears in the Cape
Estates Death Notice Index, corroborating MOOC 6/9/17017 independently.
The same database returns living Lerena daughters under married surnames
with dates of birth. Those are deliberately NOT committed here or
published; the site says so explicitly.

commits.subject: 1881/1883 sweep: A, B, C complete. New lead: the political-refugee story
commits.body:
Extends the Rosario index sweep to the years either side of 1882, since
the passport's birth date is the only authority for that year and was
written 58 years after the fact. A, B and C are clear for both 1881 and
1883 - six bands, no Pablo Armando.
Records an important caveat: the viewer presents this film under two
different image-numbering schemes (718 vs 655) with a NON-constant
offset. Image numbers are locators only; every page is verified on
arrival by letter, year, Libro and folio, and that is what the coverage
files record.
New from the family: David's mother repeated the story that Pablo
Armando fled Argentina as a communist on the run. Written up as
hypothesis 6 and in notes/communist-story.md. It is the only family story
that explains a departure. The communist label is almost certainly a
later relabel - the Argentine party dates from 1918 and he left c.1903-05,
when the movement was anarchist. The testable mechanism is Ley 4144, the
Ley de Residencia, which deported foreign-born agitators without trial -
and which applied only to FOREIGNERS, so if he was expelled he was not
Argentine-born, and his absence from the Rosario register becomes a
consequence rather than a puzzle.

commits.subject: Finish CEMLA: LERINA read, register extended to 70
commits.body:
LERINA returns four people - a single Italian household arriving together
on the ADELAIDE LAVARELLO in 1889. A different surname, marked excluded.
Corrects the register's earliest-arrival claim: the earliest arrival of a
Lerena, Llerena or Larena is 1905; the only earlier hit under any
spelling is that Italian Lerina family. Either way the conclusion stands
and is now stated precisely on /register/, /searched/ and /roadmap/ -
Pablo Armando's parents cannot be in this index.
Marks CEMLA done on the searched page and closes roadmap route 3.

commits.subject: CEMLA run + a name register of every Lerena encountered
commits.body:
CEMLA (Centro de Estudios Migratorios Latinoamericanos), the Buenos Aires
immigrant arrival index, searched across LERENA / LLERENA / LARENA with
David completing the CAPTCHAs. Results recorded in full.
The most useful result is negative: the earliest arrival under any
spelling is 1905, so no Lerena entered Argentina as a recorded immigrant
before Pablo Armando was born in 1882. His parents are not in this index.
Positives worth keeping:
- Gilberto Lerena, ARGENTINE, b. c.1879, comercio, arriving 1928 with a
  son of the same name - not among the children of the Gilberto (b.1854)
  who headed the 1895 Buenos Aires household and co-founded the
  Argentine Stud Book
- Carlos Lerena (Uruguayan, b. c.1885) with Rosa M. E. Lerena
  (Argentine), arriving together from Montevideo 1926
- Josefina Llerena, Argentine woman of property, three crossings
- Spanish bearers cluster hard on Logrono, La Rioja
New: /register/ - a working register of all 66 Lerenas met anywhere,
each with its source and an honest mark of Connected, Excluded, or
Unplaced. Nothing is claimed as kin. When Pablo Armando's parents are
finally named, this is the list that should snap into place.

commits.subject: Complete the 1882 Rosario index sweep: all 26 letters, no Pablo Armando
commits.body:
Finishes P through Z. The sweep of DGS 4530325 for the given name Pablo
Armando under any surname is now complete across every letter section of
the Rosario cathedral baptism index for 1882. He is not there.
- P 503-505, Q 548-549, R 563-565, S 612-614, T 654, U 678, V 684-685,
  W 705, Y 707, Z 708
- There is no X section in the index at all
- K and Y contain no 1882 entries whatsoever
- Eleven near misses logged and excluded, closest being Ronillon /
  Armando Juan / Libro 24 f.498
Records the negative honestly on /searched/ and /roadmap/: what it rules
out (baptism at Rosario cathedral in 1882 under any surname, this being
the only parish before 1888 and predating civil registration) and what it
does not (a different given name, a different year, a different place).
Marks the mother's-surname theory as tested-and-unrewarded, and the F
section's clearance as disposing of the Fernandez hypothesis.
Names the successor route: the same sweep across 1881 and 1883, now cheap
because every letter's position in the film is mapped.

commits.subject: Sweep 1882: sixteen sections clear, and K has no 1882 at all
commits.body:
Carried the sweep from H through O. A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, J, K, L,
Ll, M, N and O are now read in full for the year 1882, and there is no
Pablo Armando in any of them.
K is worth a note of its own: the section jumps from Libro 24 in 1881
straight to Libro 26 in 1883, so there were no K baptisms at all at this
parish in 1882. The letter is that rare in Rosario.
M turned out to be enormous, running from about image 411 to 473, and its
1882 band alone took three openings. The second volume of the index opens
at image 410 with its own title card - Indice Bautismos, Volumen M-Q, anos
1879-1900 - which confirms the film's structure and means R to Z sits in a
third volume further on.
Two more near misses joined the list and were excluded: a Pablo J. among
the G's and a Pablo Eduardo at folio 555. That makes eight near hits
across the sweep, none of them him, which continues to say the method
catches the name when it is present.
What remains is P, Q, R, S, T, U, V and W to Z. P and S are the large ones.

commits.subject: Publish everything that led nowhere
commits.body:
David asks that the searches be recorded on the site itself, not only in
