the working notes, even where they found nothing. That is right for this
archive, and there is now a Searched page carrying all of it.
Most genealogical work is negative, and knowing a register has been read
line by line and does not contain a name is worth as much as finding one -
provided somebody wrote it down. Nobody does, which is why the same
fruitless afternoon gets spent again a decade later.
So the page lists the fourteen years of Rosario baptisms, the twelve
letters of the 1882 sweep and the letters still outstanding, the six near
misses that show the sweep would catch the name if it were there, and the
control search that proves those registers are unindexed rather than
merely unsearched. It lists the indexes that came back empty, and it
separates them by reason - not there, not indexed, not digitised,
restricted, or blocked - because a record that does not exist and a record
nobody has scanned are different problems with different solutions.
It also records what was chased and abandoned: the San Miguel baptisms
David himself marks unproven, the Fernandez hypothesis that grew from them
and died in the F section, the truncated "Ler" line that would not
resolve, the second-parish idea that was reasonable for a day and wrong,
and the Find a Grave memorial that turns out to derive from the same
passport rather than corroborate it.
And it says what the failures add up to, which is not nothing: three
independent bodies of evidence decline to place this family at Rosario,
and there is no civil fallback because provincial registration did not yet
exist. His South American origin rests entirely on his own passport. The
record has not contradicted him; it has refused to agree.

commits.subject: Sweep 1882: twelve letters clear, and six near misses that prove the method
commits.body:
Carried the sweep through G, H and into I. A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, L and
Ll are now read in full for 1882 and there is no Pablo Armando in any of
them. I is located but its 1882 band, at images 346 to 347, is not yet
read.
The letter positions are now firm rather than estimated, and are recorded
with the bracketing samples that fixed them, so the remainder can be
picked up cold without re-deriving anything.
Six near misses have surfaced across the sweep - a Chaparro called Pablo
H., a Funes called Armando, an Eduardo called Paul marked natural, a
Gorosito called Pablo in the wrong year, a Pablo J. among the G's, and a
Pablo among the I's in 1884. None of them is him. Their value is
methodological: six near hits show the sweep catches the name when it is
there, so a null result at the end of it will mean something rather than
nothing.
What remains is I, J and K, then M through Z, perhaps fifteen to
twenty-five more reads, with P and S the large ones to do first if it is
ever cut short.
Recorded also, because it shaped how this was done: Chrome dropped twice
during the sitting and the viewer sometimes renders a page behind the
number requested, which costs re-reads but loses nothing - and is why the
map is written after each letter rather than at the end.

commits.subject: Sweep 1882: nine letters read, and the index turns out to flag illegitimacy
commits.body:
Kept going. A, B, C, D, E and F are now read in full for 1882, joining L
and Ll from this morning, and G is half done. There is no Pablo Armando in
any of them.
Two things learned along the way make the rest of the sweep sharper. The
index marks illegitimate births with "(N.)" for natural - there is an
"Eduardo, Paul (N.)" at folio 505 - so if Pablo Armando was born outside
marriage and registered under his mother's name, his entry should carry
that mark, and it is a second thing to scan for rather than relying on the
given name alone. And "Exposito" turns out to be a surname in its own
right here, the name given to foundlings, of which there are many; the E
section is now read and none of them is him.
Four near misses are recorded so nobody chases them twice: a Chaparro
called Pablo H., a Funes called Armando, an Eduardo called Paul and marked
natural, and a Gorosito called Pablo in the wrong year. None is him - but
that all four surfaced is the useful part, because it shows the sweep is
sensitive enough to catch the name if it is there at all.
What remains is the tail of G, then H through Z, perhaps twenty-five to
thirty-five more image reads. The letter positions are recorded so the
next session can go straight to each 1882 band.

commits.subject: Begin reading 1882 across the letters; the Fernandez idea fails
commits.body:
Proceeded with the read. The point of it is to test whether Pablo Armando
sits in the Rosario baptism index under a surname that is not Lerena -
because a child born outside marriage was commonly registered under his
mother's name, and this family's documented habit was children first and
marriage afterwards.
F is now read in full for 1882, across image 239's right page and the
whole of 240, covering Libro 24 to folio 577 and Libro 25 to folio 218.
There is no Pablo Armando in it, so the Fernandez hypothesis that David's
own tree leans on does not hold at this parish for this year. One
curiosity worth recording rather than chasing: a Funes child called
Armando at folio 163, which is an Armando but neither the right surname
nor the right given name.
C is partly read - folios 95 to 244 at image 118, with no Pablo - and
folios 1 to 94 at image 117 still to do. L and Ll were already read this
morning.
The rest is mapped rather than read, and the note says so plainly: three
letters of twenty-six. Sampled positions are recorded so each letter's
1882 band can be found in one jump, since every letter's section runs
chronologically and 1882 therefore sits early in it. Completing the sweep
is a defined job of perhaps forty to sixty more image reads at one call
each, and it would settle conclusively whether he was baptised at Rosario
in 1882 under any surname at all.

commits.subject: Send the army letter, and decline the CAPTCHA
commits.body:
David asked for both CEMLA and the letter tonight. One of those I did.
The letter has gone to the Archivo General del Ejercito at
age@ejercito.mil.ar, an address verified against argentina.gob.ar rather
than guessed - the Ministry of Defence's own archive directory, which also
confirms they offer reference at a distance by email. It was sent from
David's own account so the reply reaches him, and it asks for four things:
whether the legajo survives, the names of Pablo Armando's parents, the
military district of enrolment, and what a copy would cost. It explains
why the archive is being troubled at all - the parish index read year by
year from 1882 to 1895, the cathedral being Rosario's only parish until
1888, his absence from the 1895 census, and the fact that no provincial
civil registry existed in 1882. The message id is recorded with the
request so the thread can be found again.
CEMLA I did not run. Its search form is behind a CAPTCHA, and completing
those is precisely the check meant to establish that a person is present,
so it is not mine to defeat. It stays a five-minute job for David and the
five exact searches are written out.
Also mapped, for the route that reads 1882 across every letter rather than
only L: D sits at image 201 of the baptism index and F at 255, both in
1889-90, so F for 1882 lies around images 240 to 248. That is where a
Fernandez child called Pablo Armando would be, if David's own hypothesis
about the mother's surname is right.

commits.subject: A roadmap, and the theory that would explain three refusals
commits.body:
The Argentine record has now declined three times - fourteen years of
cathedral baptisms, the whole FamilySearch index, and the 1895 national
census - and there is no civil fallback, because Argentine civil
registration only began around 1886. For a birth in February 1882 the
parish register is the only record that could ever have existed.
So the roadmap opens with the theory that would explain all three at once.
This family's documented practice was to have children first and marry
later: Roque was born in November 1905 and his parents did not marry until
September 1911, the register calling them bachelor and spinster, with the
child baptised that June and the mother received into the church in
December. In Spanish parish and civil practice a child born outside
marriage is commonly registered under the mother's surname. If Pablo
Armando was himself born that way, he was born at Rosario exactly as his
passport says and is simply not under L - and his passport carries one
surname where Spanish practice gives two. David's own tree already leans
this way, with a Lerena mother and a Llorens father.
Seven routes are ranked by what they would settle, and marked by what they
need. Two are letters, one is five minutes at a keyboard behind a CAPTCHA,
one is the untried remount idea, one is forty page-openings of an index
already open, one is Uruguay, and one is a curiosity: both younger sons
appear in an LDS South African Mission census of 1935 indexed as "Son",
which means a head of household stands on that page giving his own
birthplace five years before the passport and independent of it. The image
is not published.
Tonight's search also confirmed the Forbes-Chappell identity from a third
source, and put Roque in the Orange Free State in 1932 through an infant
death at Bloemfontein.

commits.subject: There is no civil fallback for 1882, and the ships may be the wrong ships
commits.body:
Two findings, and three letters ready to send.
The first is structural and closes a door properly rather than leaving it
ajar. Argentine civil registration only began around 1886, so for a birth
at Rosario in February 1882 the parish register is the only record that
could ever have existed - and this archive has read that parish's index
line by line from 1882 to 1895. There is no provincial civil act to go and
order. That is not a gap in the searching; it is the shape of the Argentine
record system, and it narrows the choice hard: either he was baptised
somewhere other than Rosario, or he was not born there.
The second answers David's question about ship records by dropping an
assumption. We have been looking for a passenger, and he may never have
been one. The South African War shipped some 360,000 horses into the
country with Argentina among the main sources; he was seventeen when it
began and twenty when it ended, a horseman by trade and a horse-dealer at
the Cape by 1911. Horses travel with conductors, grooms and muleteers
engaged at the port of loading, and those men are written down in military
remount paperwork rather than civilian passenger lists - which would
explain why he is invisible in the passenger indexes. The Remount
Department series at Kew, the Cape depots at Stellenbosch and the British
purchasing commissions at Buenos Aires have none of them been touched.
Also checked and recorded so it is not tried twice: FamilySearch's indexed
military records return zero for the surname, so the libreta de
enrolamiento is an email to Buenos Aires rather than a search. That letter
is drafted in Spanish. So is the CEMLA brief, which David has to run
himself because the form is behind a CAPTCHA.

commits.subject: The 1895 census answers a different question, and a route out of Argentina
commits.body:
Searched the Argentine national census of 1895, which is indexed. It
produced one substantial Lerena household - and it is not his.
Gilberto Lerena, head, forty-one, born in Uruguay in 1854, living in
Buenos Aires with nine others in Seccion 21, Subdivision 15. The
Uruguayan records already held give Gilberto Lerena married to Julia
Salvanach with sons Carlos Augusto Federico and Raul, born at Montevideo
in 1883 and 1885; here they are ten years on. So the co-founder of the
Argentine Stud Book was a Uruguayan, born 1854, which fits a Group 1 race
being renamed for him in 1914 at or just after his death. The children's
birthplaces even date the family's move: Uruguay through 1887, Buenos
Aires from 1889.
Pablo Armando is not in that household, and not in the census at all
though he would have been thirteen. Nor is there a single Lerena recorded
in Santa Fe or Rosario. That is now the third independent body of evidence
to decline to place this family there, after fourteen years of cathedral
baptisms and the whole FamilySearch index - while Uruguay keeps answering.
The Argentina page now carries a research plan rather than a shrug. The
two best routes are implied by the passport itself: his libreta de
enrolamiento, since enrolment records name a man's parents and birthplace
and he belongs to the conscription class of 1882; and the matricula
consular the Cape Town consulate must have held on him to issue a passport
at all. Then Santa Fe's provincial civil registration, which is not online
in any form. Then Uruguay, which on this evidence is not a fallback but
the likelier answer.
And one question of its own: this family named a son Gilberto Lerena in
1957, three generations after leaving. Either they were kin to the man in
the stud book, or they knew exactly who he was.

commits.subject: A hero for the home page, and the label it needs
commits.body:
David generated the Cape stable-yard image rather than the Argentine river
one, and it is the better picture for this archive anyway: it is the yard
at Rugby that the 1931 building file records, the trade that four separate
documents attest, and the mountain he died under.
The home page is rebuilt on the Defranceschi hero pattern - full-bleed
banner with the kicker, title and standfirst overlaid, then an opener
stating who the archive is for and the two rules, then three doors into
the line, the passport and the hypotheses. Below that the four family
traditions with their verdicts, six numbers that each link to the page
earning them, and a closing section saying plainly where the line stops.
The image is captioned rather than left to speak for itself. An archive
that labels every claim cannot leave its own illustration unlabelled, so
the caption says three things: that it is a modern painted impression and
not a photograph, that it is not a picture of any building this family is
known to have owned, and that the signature in its corner is the
generator's invention and not a real artist's. The source file is kept
alongside the published webp.

commits.subject: Bring the site onto the Defranceschi Archive's design system
commits.body:
The Lerena site had its own ad-hoc theme and did not read as a sibling of
the Defranceschi archive. It now uses the same design system rather than
an approximation of it: the stylesheet is copied wholesale, and the layout
and every page have been rewritten to its vocabulary.
That means EB Garamond over Libre Franklin over IBM Plex Mono, the same
ink-and-panel palette in both light and dark, the same letterspaced
eyebrow above a large serif title, the same page head with rule beneath,
the same grouped dropdown navigation and mobile drawer, the same panels,
tables, notes and section rules - and, most importantly for an archive of
this kind, the same three confidence chips: Documented, Inferred, Family
lore. A reader moving between the two archives should not have to relearn
anything, least of all how confidence is signalled.
All fourteen pages were converted: headings and standfirsts lifted into
the layout's title, eyebrow and dek props, content split into sections,
and the old class names mapped across.
Two standfirsts were also stale and are corrected. The home page no
longer says the archive begins almost empty, which stopped being true
several hours ago, and the sources page no longer describes itself as
being on day one.

commits.subject: Uruguay is empty too, and a note on the name Carmen
commits.body:
Searched fuzzily on both names across the whole index for births between
1878 and 1886 - a Uruguay filter with a date range returns nothing at all,
so the filter was dropped and everything searched instead. Two records
come back for this man and only two: his 1911 marriage at Wynberg, and a
Find a Grave entry giving his dates without a burial place. Every other
Pablo Lerena in the window is demonstrably someone else, chief among them
a Pablo Timoteo Lerena Munoz of Atienza in Guadalajara.
So there is no South American record of Pablo Armando Lerena in the
largest genealogical index in the world. Set beside fourteen clean years
of Rosario baptisms, that means his South American origin now rests
entirely on his own passport. That is not a reason to doubt the passport,
which he swore at a consulate and which names a city, a province and a
day. It is a reason to accept that the corroborating record may simply not
be digitised, since Uruguayan and Argentine coverage is patchy and
Rosario's civil registration is unindexed for the 1880s.
David asks whether the name Carmen, in his aunt Patricia Carmen Lerena,
is a clue. On its own, barely - it is among the commonest female names in
the Spanish-speaking world and this family was Catholic. But the family's
surviving female Spanish names are scarce where the male ones are
abundant, and neither of Patricia's grandmothers, an Englishwoman of Devon
and an Afrikaner, was a Carmen. Spanish custom names children for
grandparents, so if it descends at all it descends from further back on
the Lerena side. Recorded as a modest inference and, more usefully, as a
filter: weight any Argentine or Uruguayan Lerena household containing a
Carmen.

commits.subject: Fourteen consecutive years of Rosario baptisms, and he is not in them
commits.body:
First established that these years cannot be searched: a control query for
Lopez at Rosario between 1888 and 1892 returns nothing, so the cathedral's
nineteenth-century baptisms are unindexed and only the 1910s material is
searchable. They had to be read.
Images 377 to 393 of the baptism index are now read, covering Libros 24 to
38 and the years 1885 through 1895. With this morning's work that makes
1882 to 1895 - fourteen consecutive years - together with the whole Ll-
section for 1880 to 1884. There is no Lerena in any of it. The L pages are
thick with Rosario's actual L families, the same names recurring year on
year: Lopez, Lucero, Luduena, Leguizamon, Luraschi, Lencina, Ledesma,
Leiva, Lescano, Lanfranconi, Lavena. Lerena is simply not among them.
Three gaps are stated rather than glossed: image 392 was not opened, the
lower halves of 387 and 389 rendered blurred because the tiles did not
load, and 1896 to 1900 is unread. None is likely to matter, since a
baptism at twelve or older is improbable and the run is otherwise
unbroken.
Set against the parish finding - that the cathedral was Rosario's only
church until 1888 - the conclusion is that the Rosario baptism should now
be treated as unlikely to exist at all. The effort moves to whether he was
born at Rosario in the first place. His passport says so and it is his own
document, but nothing corroborates it, and there is a Rosario in Uruguay,
in the country where this surname is densest and where Montevideo Lerenas
are already surfacing in every search.

commits.subject: Rosario had one parish in 1882, so the clean index means much more
commits.body:
Went looking for a Lerena baptism at Santa Rosa de Lima, the second
Rosario parish found this morning, and checked when that parish began. The
answer reverses this morning's reasoning.
Santa Rosa de Lima did not become a parish until 19 February 1888, and its
first baptism was performed that day; before then Rosario had, in the
words of the parish's own history, only the cathedral. San Jose and
Inmaculada Concepcion are later still and appear in the indexed records
only from the 1910s.
So in February 1882 the cathedral was the only parish in Rosario. This
archive has read its baptism index line by line for 1882, 1883, 1884 and
1885, together with the whole Ll- section for 1880 to 1884, and found no
Lerena and no Llerena. Those two facts together say something much
stronger than "he was probably baptised elsewhere in Rosario": he was not
baptised in Rosario at all in those years, because there was nowhere else
in Rosario to be baptised. The other-parish hypothesis, raised only hours
ago, is closed - a reasonable idea, and wrong for these years.
Four possibilities survive, and the cheapest is a late baptism after 1885,
which this family's own habits support since Pablo Armando's son Roque was
born in 1905 and baptised in 1911. The same index runs to 1900. Failing
that, he was christened in another town, or he was not born at Rosario at
all - and there is a Rosario in Uruguay, in the country where the surname
is densest, though his passport says Rosario de Santa Fe explicitly.
The search also turned up a Bartolome Llerena in the 1869 census at
Rosario, born in Cordoba in 1824, and several Llorens families at the
Rosario parishes - which is presumably why the 1872 San Miguel baptism
looked plausible, though it remains unproven and Buenos Aires-based.

commits.subject: Read image 51, and find the better method underneath it
commits.body:
Chrome came back and image 51 of the marriage index was read properly:
pages 150 and 151, Libro 8 and Libro 9, under year headings running 1876
to 1885 - the whole window that matters - with dozens of L surnames.
One candidate came out of it and it is not confirmed. Under Libro 9, 1884,
a line reads "Larena V, Sarmiento A, 20", and at the best resolution
available I cannot tell Larena from Lavena or Lerena. Lavena is a real
Rosario surname, so it is recorded as a candidate only, to be settled at
folio 20 of the 1884-1891 marriage register. If it does prove to be
Lerena, the date is worth noting: 1884, two years after Pablo Armando's
birth, which is exactly the pattern his own son shows.
The more valuable find was underneath. Opening that register revealed an
image-index panel tabulating every act with the names and ages of the
parties and, crucially, the names of both parents. These registers are
indexed. Reading handwriting was never necessary, and a surname search
returns six thousand Lerena records for Argentina and seven hundred and
thirty for Santa Fe.
Searching them immediately produced the thing four clean years at the
cathedral had implied: a second Rosario parish with Lerenas in it. Carmen
Roman Lerena was baptised at Santa Rosa de Lima, Rosario, in 1918, her
mother a Manuela Lerena. It also turned up an Armando Lerena baptised at
Santa Fe city in 1917 to Casimiro Lerena and Amelia Lepiani, and it
documented the Montevideo Lerena Lenguas - Luis Serena Lenguas and Julia
Juanico, with a Justiniana Lenguas in the family - which is plainly where
Gilberto Justiniano Lerena Lenguas of the Argentine Stud Book gets his
names, and makes that a Montevideo family rather than an Argentine one.
One trap recorded: there is a Rosario in Uruguay as well.

commits.subject: The marriage index narrows to a single page
commits.body:
Third pass, and a better door. Navigating the ark directly rather than the
film number resolves to a named waypoint - Rosario, Nuestra Senora del
Rosario, "Indice de matrimonios 1860-1904" - of only 88 images, half the
size of the film listing and scoped exactly to the period in question.
Within it, image 51 carries the L surnames under year headings for 1878,
1880, 1881 and 1883, with the 1860s and 1870s on the pages immediately
before. Pablo Armando was born in February 1882, so his parents married
before that: image 51, and its neighbours at 49, 50 and 52, is the page.
Luraschi, Lucero, Luduena, Lopez, Lucas, Lara, Laguna and Lorenzo are all
legible there. Lerena was not positively identified, but the page was
never rendered sharply enough to exclude it either.
The stop is now plainly a tooling limit rather than anything about the
records. Chrome disconnected mid-task and did not return, and Chrome was
the only surface where the region-zoom action works - which is what makes
this handwriting legible. The in-app browser pane cannot region-crop at
all, and at its width the deep-zoom tiles blur before the script can be
read.
So the page is identified, open and unrestricted, and the instructions for
reading it are written down: the waypoint ark, image 51, Chrome, fit zoom,
region crops on quarters. The line will give the groom's surname, the
bride's surname and a page number, and that number opens the marriage
register for 1868-1884 or 1853-1867.

commits.subject: Second run at the marriage index: legibility solved, navigation defeated
commits.body:
Went back at DGS 4531036 and got the reading problem the right way round.
The mistake last time was zooming the viewer in, which makes the page
wider than the viewport and pushes the groom's surname column off-screen
to the left. At the viewer's fit zoom, a region crop of the left page
renders this handwriting perfectly, and the exact regions are now written
into the queue.
That let me confirm the letter positions properly rather than by
estimate - D at image 49 with Duarte, Durand and Dominguez, F at 59 with
Franco and Fonseca, J at 72, P at 90 - which keeps L bracketed to images
76 to 84.
What stopped it was the viewer rather than the film. On this particular
roll it gets into a stuck state: URL navigation lands in thumbnail mode
and the thumbnails sometimes never load; the single-page toggle does not
open the requested image but snaps back to the last single-page image
viewed; and once stuck, both the image-number box and the forward and back
arrows stop responding, so only image 49 would render. A fresh page load
clears it, and that is the instruction left for next time - open the film
in a new tab, switch to single-page view first, and use the number box
before touching anything else.
The pages are located, unrestricted and legible. They were simply never
put on screen.

commits.subject: Decode the marriage index and pin the L section to eight pages
commits.body:
Opened the Rosario marriage index, DGS 4531036, and worked out how it is
built. It is a different animal from the baptism index: 180 images against
718, handwritten rather than typed, alphabetical by surname but
sub-divided by year within each surname group, with the occasional Libro
heading. The columns give the groom's surname, the bride's surname and a
page number, so a single line names both families - which is why this
index is worth more than the baptism one for a man whose parents are
unknown.
Located it by sampling: J at image 72 with Jurgens, Juary and Juriol, and
P at image 90 with Pacheco, Palma, Paz, Perez and Peralta. So L sits at
roughly images 76 to 84, and image 78 already shows the right kind of
content.
Not read yet, and I want to be plain about why: the stopping point is
mechanical rather than evidential. This index is fainter than the baptism
one and needs more magnification, and at that magnification the page runs
wider than the viewport so the groom's surname column falls off to the
left and has to be dragged into view before cropping. The images
themselves are open, unrestricted and perfectly legible at the right zoom.
The viewer mechanics are now written down so the next attempt does not
rediscover them: the plus button sits at the far right of the toolbar, and
the icon near the middle is the grid toggle that kept throwing earlier
sessions back into thumbnail view.

commits.subject: Chase the "Ler" line into the register; it does not hold
commits.body:
Followed the odd index line - "Ler, Maria, 1884, folio 13" - into the
book. Libro 27 turns out to sit on DGS 4098790, its printed cover at image
4, so the volume was easy to find. Stamped folios 11, 13 and 14 were read
off the marginal entry columns and none carries a Ler or a matching Maria:
folio 13 holds Lugardi, Zurbicki, Navarro and Bustos, folio 11 holds Villa,
Vaz and Castilla, folio 14 holds Iglesias, Guiscardo, a Maria Cadolat and
Pierra.
The foliation is the reason it cannot be pinned down. The index puts
Luzardi Juan Eugenio at folio 15, and that man is physically entry 502 on
stamped folio 13, so the index runs about two ahead - but that offset rests
on one name, and applying it did not produce the entry either. Either the
index line does not read "Ler", or its foliation diverges by more than a
constant. Recorded as a weak lead and dropped rather than pursued further.
The films are now mapped, and two things fall out. David's film 4098791 is
"Bautismos 1882-1884" - exactly the span the index has cleared - so its 543
pages would have yielded nothing, which is what the index was for. And the
better target is no longer a baptism at all: the marriage registers for
1868-1884 and 1853-1867 would give Pablo Armando's parents' marriage, which
names all four of his grandparents, and there is a marriage index to find
it with.

commits.subject: Four clean years at the cathedral, and the search moves parish
commits.body:
Carried the Rosario index on through 1884 and 1885, images 373 to 376,
reading every line of the L run: Libro 25 folios 210 to 299, Libro 26 and
27 folios 305 to 453 and 2 to 5, Libro 27 folios 12 to 359 and 363 to 656,
Libro 28 folios 2 to 127. No Lerena anywhere.
So the negative now covers 1882, 1883, 1884 and 1885 end to end, together
with the whole Ll- section for 1880 to 1884. Pablo Armando was not
baptised at Nuestra Senora del Rosario in the four years after his birth,
which is long enough to absorb even the six-year delay this family showed
with his own son. The likeliest explanation is no longer a late baptism
but a different parish, and the catalogue entry worked so far is
specifically the cathedral's.
One oddity is worth an afternoon: image 374 carries a surname written as
the bare "Ler", for a Maria baptised in 1884 at Libro 27 folio 13. It may
be nothing, or a clipped Lerena, and if it is the latter she would be a
sister. It costs one page to find out.

commits.subject: Read the Rosario index: he is not there
commits.body:
Chrome drove the deep-zoom viewer where the in-app pane could not, and the
region-zoom action renders the typescript perfectly, so the index could be
read line by line rather than guessed at.
The whole L run for 1882 and 1883 in the cathedral parish index is now
covered end to end - Libro 24 folios 402 to 574, Libro 25 folios 9 to 249
and 457 to 540, Libro 26 folios 7 to 209 - together with the entire Ll-
section for 1880 to 1884, which turns out to hold just seven entries.
There is no Lerena and no Llerena in any of it.
So Pablo Armando was not baptised at Nuestra Senora del Rosario in 1882 or
1883. That is a finding rather than a failure: the index is legible, it is
complete for those years, and it was read rather than sampled.
The most promising explanation is one the family's own records supply.
This family delayed baptisms - Pablo Armando's son Roque was born in
November 1905 and not baptised until June 1911, six years later. If the
father was treated the same way his entry lies somewhere in 1884 to 1895,
which is another dozen pages of an index already open and is much the
cheapest thing to try next. Failing that, Rosario had more than one parish
by 1882.
One consequence worth recording: David's original film is a register
volume rather than an index, and now that 1882 and 1883 are excluded at
this parish it may be the wrong volume altogether.

commits.subject: Rosario: the register need not be read, because there is an index
commits.body:
Followed David's own note to the film he had marked "still need to look
through". It is the cathedral parish of Rosario - Nuestra Senora del
Rosario, catalogue koha:208788, seventy-one rolls filmed in 1974 - and the
images are not restricted.
The useful finding is that he does not have to read it. His note points at
the register volume itself, 543 images to be turned one at a time. The
catalogue also carries separate alphabetical baptism indexes, and one of
them, DGS 4530325, covers 1879 to 1900 and therefore 1882.
Decoding that index took most of the work. Its columns are apellidos,
nombres, ano and folio, in blocks headed by Libro number, and it is
alphabetical by letter but chronological within each letter - so the L
section is a run of pages ordered by year rather than by given name. Image
403 is at 1900 and 1901, the end of that run, and image 406 has already
crossed into Ll-, which Spanish indexes place after L. So 1882 sits a few
pages earlier, around images 395 to 402. Read the Libro and folio off that
line and the register entry follows, and it names his parents.
I could not finish it myself: the deep-zoom viewer renders unreliably in
this browser pane, needing a click to draw but jumping pages when the
click lands in the image area, and flipping into thumbnail mode. That is a
tooling limit and not a records one, and the target is now narrow enough
to do by hand in a few minutes.
Two better or adjacent targets came out of the same catalogue. The
marriage index for 1860 to 1921 would give his parents' marriage, which
names both fathers and both mothers - four names where a baptism gives
two. And the baptism index for L-Z 1731 to 1879 should hold his older
siblings, and perhaps his parents' own baptisms.

commits.subject: Read David's own facts, and be corrected by them
commits.body:
A process failure worth naming: I had been reading the MyHeritage tree's
rendered cards - names and dates - and never opening the Biography, Facts
and Notes panels where David records his research. He was right to say I
would end up finding links for things he had already found. The method is
now written into the queue: re-root the tree and read the panel first,
then research beyond it.
Doing so corrects this archive in several places and hands it four new
leads.
Mary Septima Taylor was born at Bideford, Devon, on 17 September 1884,
cited to the GRO index, and christened at St Margaret's, Northam. My
doubt about her English birth lasted part of one day and rested on a
badly filtered search; it is retired as disproved rather than deleted.
Her father William Taylor, born at Worlingworth in Suffolk, was a
coachman - so the horses are on both sides of the marriage - and the
family is of Northam and Bideford, six miles apart, which is Brayley's
own country. The inference from that surname alone held.
She was a pupil teacher, awarded a diocesan prize in religious knowledge
six weeks after her mother died, at sixteen. And on 16 December 1911 she
was baptised a Catholic, three months after the wedding - so the year runs
son in June, parents in September, mother in December.
The family's memory that Pablo cut Luis off is legible in the will: Luis
took half a share, the same as a woman described as no relation, while his
two brothers held three-quarters between them. The Chappell tangle
resolves too - Roque married Rose Forbes, who was his brother's
mother-in-law, so Chappell was her name by an earlier marriage, exactly as
one of the two readings proposed.
Four new leads, all from David's notes. The consular tradition may be
Uruguayan rather than Argentine, which would explain why nothing has been
found on the Argentine side. He imported horses from Argentina for the
South African government - the testable form of the horse claim this
archive framed on day one. He held land at Blouberg that the deeds sweep
failed to find, so that sweep needs redoing under every spelling. And
David has already located the Rosario film that should name Pablo
Armando's parents.

commits.subject: Went for the passenger lists and found the marriage instead
commits.body:
Cape Province marriage register no. 160, 3 September 1911, solemnized at
Wynberg: married in St Dominic's after banns. Pablo Armando Lerena, 29,
bachelor, horse-dealer, of Diep River; Mary Septima Taylor, 27, spinster,
of Diep River. Both signed their own names in full. The examining
signature reads "Bert..." - and Bertram W. Glynn is the priest who had
baptised their son at Wynberg three months earlier.
Their first son was born on 25 November 1905, so they married nearly six
years after they became parents, and the register calls them bachelor and
spinster, meaning neither had been married before to anyone. That closes a
puzzle this archive had already noticed and could not explain: Roque's
baptism was delayed six years to June 1911, and his parents married that
September. The family was brought into the church in the course of a
single year, the child first and the parents after, apparently by the same
priest.
It also gives his trade at the earliest date yet - horse-dealer - so the
sequence now runs horse-dealer in 1911, trainer by 1940 with a yard taking
apprentices, race horse owner at death in 1950. And it adds Diep River at
the front of an address sequence that runs on through Rugby, Observatory,
Camps Bay and Newlands.
For the ship, it removes an assumption rather than the story: she was
Taylor until September 1911, so she appears under Taylor on any earlier
passenger list, and being unmarried the two may well have travelled
separately. The queue is amended accordingly.
A caution goes with it. A search of the English records returns nothing at
all for a Mary Septima Taylor born in 1884 - no birth, no baptism, no
census - only her South African marriage and death. Her English birth is
family knowledge and is now labelled as such, since she could as easily
have been born at the Cape to an English family.
Adds a hypotheses page gathering every unproved proposition the archive is
entertaining, with what suggests it, what would settle it, and what weight
it deserves - including the two now retired as disproved.

commits.subject: Mary Septima Taylor: a name that is a count, and a ship story that holds
commits.body:
Opened the Taylor side from the MyHeritage tree. The trick is to re-root
the tree with rootIndividualID on the URL and read its own data store; the
viewport loads only what it draws, so any branch has to be re-rooted to be
reached.
Mary Septima Taylor, born 17 September 1884, died 15 November 1935, was
the ninth of ten children of William Taylor and Mary Ann Hellen Brayley.
Her name is arithmetic and the arithmetic comes out: counting the
daughters in order of birth, she is the seventh, which is what Septima
means. That in turn settles something the tree leaves blank, since the
unnamed twin of 1879 must have been a girl or the count fails. The name
her parents gave their ninth child preserves a sister whose own name is
lost.
Behind her stand James Taylor, born about 1796, and Harriet Reynolds, who
died in 1827 when her son William was twenty-one months old - so the
Taylor line now reaches further back than the Lerena line, where Pablo
Armando's parents are still unknown. Birthplaces are not recorded
anywhere in the tree and are not asserted here; the English censuses of
1891 and 1901 would supply them in one line each.
On the family's own objection - she was in England, so what was he doing
on a ship out of England - three things answer it. The River Plate reached
the Cape through Europe in that decade, so he need only have changed ships
at Southampton. The South African War shipped some 360,000 horses into the
country, Argentina among the sources, and he was seventeen when it began
and twenty when it ended. And she was orphaned at fifteen and eighteen,
in the years when the Colonial Office was running an organised scheme to
send single British women to the Cape.
None of that is evidence about these two people, and the page says so.
What settles it is one class of record: the UK outward passenger lists,
indexed from 1890. Their first son was born at Cape Town in November 1905,
which brackets the crossing tightly.
Also corrects an earlier attribution: the Chappell of the racing press
attaches through Ricardo's marriage to Doreen May Chappell, not through
Roque, whose first wife the tree gives as Rosaline Wilhelmina Forbes.

commits.subject: The deeds registers: no farm, and the sixty-one are not one family
commits.body:
Read the three land records surfaced by full-text search. They are Deeds
Office transfer registers rather than farm registers, and they answer two
open questions by pointing the other way from where this archive was
leaning.
Two of the three are Nuno Fernando Lerena, identified in both by his birth
date as South African deeds records do. They are suburban erven of about
613 and 1,353 square metres - house plots, not farms - and one is dated
August 1953, close to the October 1954 in which his father's estate
capital fell due. Pablo Armando himself holds no land in these registers
at all.
That makes the ostrich farm doubtful rather than merely untested. He was a
Cape Town racing man throughout: stables at Rugby, a yard taking
apprentices, a Newlands address, Race Horse Owner on his death
certificate. It is not disproof, since deeds coverage is partial and a
farm could have been leased, and Oudtshoorn's own records remain
unsearched - but the claim now has evidence against it and none for it,
and it is the last of the four family traditions standing on nothing.
The third record is a different family entirely: the deceased estate of
Lucas Lerena, whose widow was Rachel Lerenia born Maleka, a Sotho or
Tswana surname, at B. Eaton Township. A 1939 Pretoria membership roll
carries a Hanson Seko Lerena. So this archive's day-one reading of the
sixty-one South African Lerenas as, in effect, one family was too strong.
There are at least two unconnected Lerena populations here, and the raw
figure can no longer carry the argument. The founder-cluster reading still
holds for this family, whose descent is documented, but the arithmetic
that once stood in for it is withdrawn on the page rather than quietly
removed.

commits.subject: La Rioja: the Spanish end of the name has one cluster, and it is Basque country
commits.body:
David supplied Forebears' own page, which carries the Spanish regional
split that the site's sub-page would not serve: La Rioja 27 per cent,
Andalusia 25, Madrid 19. As raw percentages those read as three
comparable strongholds. Converted to density they are nothing of the sort.
La Rioja holds the name at 1 in 1,331 - forty times the Spanish average -
against 1 in 37,848 for Andalusia and 1 in 38,255 for Madrid, which is
roughly what you would expect if Lerenas were spread evenly and those two
regions simply held a great many people. There is exactly one real Lerena
cluster in Spain and it sits on the upper Ebro.
That discriminates between the two origins this archive has carried open
since day one. If Lerena were a worn-down Llerena, the name should be
thickest around Extremadura; Extremadura does not appear in the Spanish
distribution at all. The single cluster is instead immediately south of
the Basque provinces and Navarre, exactly where Basque house-names in
-ena spill into Castilian-speaking country.
So the reading is now a Basque-formed house-name of the upper Ebro rather
than an Extremaduran toponymic - recorded as inference from distribution,
not proof from a register, which is the distinction this archive has kept
from the start. Its practical value is that the Spanish end of the search
now has a province instead of a country.
The same page also notes that Lerena is borne as a forename by 284 people,
which is precisely the trap that produced the false positive in the NAAIRS
sweep, and that is written into the queue.

commits.subject: Bob Lerena of Cape Town, and the death notice runs into a wall
commits.body:
The racing press names him outright. The Sporting Post's 2014 obituary of
the trainer Alan Higgins says Higgins rode as a schoolboy "before being
apprenticed to Bob Lerena, who was the grandfather of Spike", and that
Peter Kannemeyer was apprenticed to Bob Lerena at the same time. Spike's
grandfather is Ricardo's father, which is Pablo Armando Lerena; Bob is
Robert; Higgins was born in 1929, so the apprenticeship falls around
1944-47 and Pablo Armando died in 1950.
So he did not merely hold a passport calling him a trainer. He ran a yard
at Cape Town that took apprentices, two of whom are named and one of whom
went on to found the Philippi training centre - published, and entirely
independent of every document this archive holds. It also gives a third
form of his name: Pablo Armando at the Argentine consulate, Robert Paul
at the registry, Bob in the yard.
The death notice is blocked rather than missing. Signed in to
FamilySearch, the Cape probate collection returns "Image Restricted" -
viewable only at an affiliate library, which is presumably how the pages
already held were got. Recorded so it is not retried from home. Two routes
remain, and both are now written up as requests: an affiliate visit to
browse the film around the pages held, or an order to the Western Cape
Archives for MOOC 6/9/17017, which the liquidation account proves contains
a death notice.
Full-text search did yield two new records that are readable: Roque Luis
Armando Lerena on a South African voters' roll of 1925-31, his full name
exactly as the parish register has it; and a deeds entry naming Nuno
Fernando Lerena with his birth date, badly OCR'd and worth reading by eye.
Two further farm records are unexamined, and the ostrich farm is still an
open claim.

commits.subject: A parish register merges two men into one, and Rosario becomes the family's
commits.body:
Cheryl Defranceski obtained the baptism register of Corpus Christi,
Wynberg, and it overturns yesterday's reading. The entry for Roque Lois
Armando - born 25 November 1905, baptised 12 June 1911 - names his parents
as Pablo Armando Lerena and Mary Septima Lerena, olim Taylor. That is the
same son whose 1973 death notice gives his parents as Roberto Lerena and
Mary Septima Lerena. Same son, same mother: the father is one man under
two forms of his name, Spanish at the altar and English at the registry.
This archive had set the two side by side, failed to reconcile them, and
proposed brothers as thin inference. That inference is retracted on the
page rather than quietly removed.
The consequences are large. Generation 1 is Pablo Armando Lerena, born at
Rosario de Santa Fe on 22 February 1882 - so the family's Rosario
tradition is confirmed for the head of the line himself, from a passport
he carried, signed and pressed his thumb to, and not merely for a relative
whose papers survived. The seventy-six years on his 1950 death certificate
is therefore wrong; he was sixty-eight, and the informant was the man
causing burial rather than any kin. The Roberto of the 1973 form is
explained too: it was signed by Rhena May, Roque's second wife, who
married him in 1966 and never met his father.
Mary Septima's maiden name is now documented rather than charted - olim
Taylor - which is the Taylor of the MyHeritage tree's title.
Two new threads. The baptism was delayed six years, which would be
explained by a crossing between 1905 and 1911. And both godparents stood
by proxy under Spanish names, Jose and Maria Louisa Breton, which suggests
they were not in South Africa to stand in person.

commits.subject: The family papers close the line, and unseat the man who opened it
commits.body:
Worked through David's own Lerena documents. The descent is now continuous
and documented at every step, and the head of the family is not who this
archive said yesterday.
Generation 1 is ROBERTO PAUL LERENA, born in South America about 1874,
died at Newlands, Cape Town on 19 March 1950. His death certificate gives
his occupation as Race Horse Owner - the family's horse tradition now
attested by the state itself, alongside the 1931 stables file and, among
the debts of his estate, a claim for twenty-six pounds of carrots. His
wife Mary Septima was buried at Maitland in November 1935 aged 51,
certified by the same doctor who signed his own certificate fifteen years
later.
What identifies him is a death notice filed twenty-three years after his
own: that of his eldest son Roque Luis Armando, which answers question 19
with "Father: ROBERTO LERENA. Mother: MARY SEPTIMA LERENA." His 1950
estate then names Nuno Fernando Lerena as a residuary heir with his exact
birth date, 6 October 1924, and Nuno's own 1971 death notice names Cheryl
Ann among his children. There is no inferred link left in the descent.
This displaces Pablo Armando Lerena, who yesterday appeared to head the
line. He does not reconcile with Roberto Paul - born 1882 against about
1874, Trainer against Race Horse Owner, Pablo and Armando against Roberto
and Paul - though both are South American widowers in the horse business
living in the same small suburb. The page now sets the two men side by
side and proposes brothers, thinly and as inference. His passport keeps
its value regardless: it is the only document here naming an exact
Argentine town.
The Spanish baptisms of 1872 are recorded as unproven at David's own
instruction, with the reasons written out - the surname is Llorens, and
the streets point to Buenos Aires rather than Rosario - so the record is
not chased twice. One image in the folder is misfiled and belongs to the
Falco archive.
Above Roberto Paul there is still nothing. The death notice from his own
estate file would name his parents and birthplace, and the account proves
it was written.

commits.subject: The passport: generation 1 is named, and three claims are tested
commits.body:
An Argentine passport in the family's own papers - Serie A No. 07962,
issued at Cape Town on 24 December 1940 - names PABLO ARMANDO LERENA,
born at Rosario de Santa Fe on 22 February 1882, Argentine by birth,
living at Rugby in Cape Town, a widower, travelling to Portuguese East
Africa. His profession is given in one word: Trainer. Under military
service it records the Guardia Nacional, 6th Cavalry, 1915.
That tests the family's account rather than repeating it. Rosario is
confirmed exactly. The horses are confirmed twice over - a trainer by
trade, a cavalryman before that - and his address, Rugby, is the same
suburb as the 1931 municipal file for proposed stables at Koeberg Road
found in NAAIRS two hours earlier, from a different archive. The consular
claim goes the other way: he is the bearer here, and the signature in the
consul's box is A. B. Bayne, Encargado. It is demoted to disputed, with
the honorary-consul hypothesis - recorded before this document surfaced -
still open.
MyHeritage, reachable once the extension connected, closes the middle.
Nuno Fernando Lerena (1924-1971) married Catherine Mary Sophia Booyzen
and is Cheryl Anne Lerena's father; the tree and the deceased-estate file
MHG 6746/71 name the same widow independently, and Booyzen is the
Afrikaans surname this archive predicted from the tree's title before
reading either.
What is still missing is the join between generations 1 and 2. That Nuno
is Pablo Armando's son is the obvious reading and not yet a document, and
whether Pablo Armando is also the "Robert Paul Lerena" whose estate opened
in 1950 is left open on the page rather than assumed. The Cape estate file
MOOC 6/9/17017 settles both, and names parents and birthplace besides.

commits.subject: NAAIRS answers: six names, a set of stables, and an estate file
commits.body:
Searched the South African National Archives index for the surname across
all repositories. Thirteen documents, twelve of them genuine, and the
archive goes from having no names at all to having six.
Cape Town holds one man across five files. Robert Paul Lerena submitted
plans for STABLES at Koeberg Road, Rugby in 1931 - the first hard
corroboration of the horse tradition, a municipal building file rather
than a memory - and was still improving that property in 1950, the year
his estate was opened. MOOC 6/9/17017 is now the highest-value document
in the project: a Cape estate file of that period carries the death
notice, which names parents and birthplace. If he was born in Argentina,
that is where it will say so.
The record then moves to the Transvaal, which is the family reaching the
Rand. Two more deceased estates name Nuno Fernando Lerena (d. 1971) and
Roque Luis Armando Lerena (d. 1973) with their widows, and divorce files
add Ricardo Paul and Anton Armando.
The given names are the real finding. Nuno is distinctly Portuguese;
Roque, Luis, Armando and Ricardo are Spanish or Portuguese - borne by men
living in South Africa and marrying Corbetts and Boltons. A family still
naming sons this way generations after arriving knows where it came from,
and that supports the River Plate origin from a government index rather
than from the family's own account.
Two useful negatives: LLERENA returns nothing, so there is no spelling
variant to chase here; and no Lerena gravestones are indexed.
Nothing is yet tied to Cheryl Anne Lerena. Six names are now orderable;
the link to David's own line is not made, and none is drawn.
Adds tools/naairs.py, which carries the session token through the legacy
CGI flow so the search can be repeated.

commits.subject: Establish the Lerena archive on its baseline
commits.body:
Day one. The line itself is three generations deep and only one of them
has a name, so this commit publishes the baseline rather than a pedigree,
and labels every family claim as testimony.
The surname is the finding. Lerena has 2,124 bearers worldwide - 22x
scarcer than Falco - which inverts the method: rarity lets distribution
propose connections, though only registers may prove them. Uruguay holds
the world's highest density (1:7,962, ~6.6x Spain's), making the River
Plate the heartland and corroborating the family's Rosario tradition
independently of it. South Africa's 61 bearers are ~3% of every Lerena
alive, in a country with no Spanish colonial past: the signature of one
family arriving and multiplying.
Two documented Lerenas sit in the bloodstock world the family remembers.
Gilberto Justiniano Lerena Lenguas co-founded the Argentine Stud Book and
has a Group 1 at Palermo named for him since 1914; Gavin Lerena rides in
South Africa. No relationship is claimed.
The name may be two names - Basque -ena, "the house of", or a reduction
of Llerena in Badajoz - and that fork is left open.
Assessed rather than repeated: "brought racing to South Africa" cannot
stand literally, so the three testable forms are recorded instead; the
ostrich farm carries a district and a date with it (Oudtshoorn, and the
feather boom's collapse in 1914); and since Oudtshoorn is far from any
capital, the consulship was plausibly honorary - which would reconcile a
diplomat with a horse-breeder and explain absence from career lists.
Generation 1 has no name, and that blocks everything downstream.
